# Assassination of George Lincoln Rockwell
## 1\. Introduction
On the afternoon of August 25, 1967, the volatile and theatrical career of George Lincoln Rockwell, the founder and Commander of the American Nazi Party (ANP), was brought to a violent conclusion in the parking lot of a suburban shopping center in Arlington, Virginia . Rockwell, a figure who had spent nearly a decade cultivating a persona of "calculated offensiveness" to thrust his fringe ideology into the national spotlight, was shot dead while sitting in his vehicle outside a laundromat . The assassination was not the work of the many political enemies Rockwell had made among Jewish groups, civil rights organizations, or the federal government, but rather an act of fratricide committed by John Patler, a former captain in his own paramilitary organization .

The murder of Rockwell marked a definitive watershed moment in the history of the American radical right. It effectively ended the era of "Rockwellism"—a strategy characterized by open, public agitation, media manipulation, and the attempt to veneer National Socialism with a uniquely American, populist aesthetic . In the immediate aftermath, the movement he founded descended into a chaotic struggle for succession, characterized by the fracturing of the party into competing sects, the rise of "esoteric" Hitlerism under his successor Matt Koehl, and a shift from public political theater to underground revolutionary terror .

This report provides a comprehensive examination of the assassination, reconstructing the minute-by-minute details of the event, the psychological profile of the assassin, the bizarre legal and political standoff regarding Rockwell’s funeral, and the complex judicial proceedings that followed. Furthermore, it analyzes the long-term sociological and political impacts of the event, exploring how the decapitation of the American Nazi Party catalyzed the evolution of modern white supremacist movements in the United States.

## 2\. Historical and Biographical Context
### 2.1 George Lincoln Rockwell: The "American Fuehrer"
To understand the significance of the assassination, one must examine the victim's trajectory. Born in Bloomington, Illinois, in 1918, George Lincoln Rockwell was the son of vaudeville performers—a biographical detail that historians frequently cite as the origin of his flare for dramatic political stunts . Unlike the stereotypical image of a marginalized extremist, Rockwell possessed a pedigree of mainstream success; he was a student at Brown University (though he dropped out to join the Navy) and a talented commercial artist .

Rockwell’s military service was distinguished. He served as a pilot in the U.S. Navy during World War II and was recalled to duty for the Korean War, rising to the rank of Commander . It was during his naval service in San Diego in the 1950s that Rockwell became radicalized, absorbing antisemitic literature and eventually concluding that Adolf Hitler was a misunderstood savior of the white race .

In 1958, Rockwell founded the organization that would become the American Nazi Party. He established its headquarters in a farmhouse at 928 North Randolph Street in Arlington, Virginia . This location, fortified and frequently draped in swastika banners, earned the local moniker "Hatemonger Hill" and became a focal point of tension in the quiet, middle-class suburb just across the Potomac from Washington, D.C..1

Rockwell’s strategy was predicated on the belief that "negative publicity is better than no publicity." He utilized his skills in commercial art and advertising to create provocative imagery and slogans . He traveled to university campuses, such as the University of Michigan, where he engaged in debates that were often less about persuasion and more about spectacle . In these settings, he openly acknowledged his lack of popularity, telling audiences, "I do not expect to make any converts here," while simultaneously predicting that economic collapse and racial warfare would eventually drive the American populace to seek his leadership .

### 2.2 The American Nazi Party (ANP) Structure
By 1967, the ANP—later rebranded as the National Socialist White People's Party (NSWPP)—remained a "modestly sized" organization . Despite Rockwell’s claims of a growing legion of stormtroopers, the core membership was relatively small, often living communally in the "barracks" at the Arlington headquarters .

The internal culture of the party was paramilitary and strictly hierarchical. Members wore uniforms, addressed Rockwell as "Commander," and adhered to a rigid schedule of training and indoctrination. However, the organization was also plagued by financial instability and constant legal pressure. The car Rockwell drove on the day of his death—a "fading blue-and-white 1958 Chevrolet"—was emblematic of the party's actual material conditions: aging, worn, and far less imposing than the image projected in their propaganda .

### 2.3 John Patler: The Disillusioned Disciple
The man who would pull the trigger, John Patler, represented the internal contradictions of the movement Rockwell attracted. Born John Christ Patsalos in New York City on January 6, 1938, Patler’s early life was defined by tragedy and violence . When he was five years old, his father shot and killed his mother, a trauma that shadowed his development . Following a turbulent adolescence marked by criminal convictions and mental health issues, Patler served in the U.S. Marines from 1958 to 1960 .

Patler joined the ANP in 1960, changing his name from Patsalos to Patler to sound more "American" and less ethnic . He was a talented artist and served as the editor and cartoonist for the party’s publication, *The Stormtrooper*.2 For years, he was one of Rockwell’s closest confidants, rising to the number-four position in the party hierarchy .

However, Patler’s standing was precarious. His Greek heritage made him a target for the "Hitler purists" within the party, who adhered to a strict definition of Aryanism that favored Nordic traits . Patler was often derided as a "greasy Greek" by other members, creating a fissure between him and the blonde ideal espoused by the leadership . While Rockwell initially protected him, the racial ideology they both espoused eventually turned inward.

## 3\. Prelude to Assassination: The Schism of 1967
### 3.1 The "Bolshevik" Accusation and Expulsion
In early 1967, the tensions between Patler and the party leadership reached a breaking point. Despite Patler’s contributions—including his advocacy for renaming the party to the NSWPP to broaden its appeal—Rockwell moved to purge him from the ranks .

In March 1967, Rockwell formally expelled Patler . The official reasons given were "Bolshevik leanings"—an accusation of Marxist sympathies that was the ultimate heresy in a National Socialist organization—and creating dissension between "dark-haired and blond Nazis" . This expulsion was not merely an administrative action; it was a total excommunication from the social and economic support system Patler had relied on for seven years.

### 3.2 Escalation and Humiliation
Following the expulsion, the relationship between the two men deteriorated into open hostility. Rockwell, seemingly intent on enforcing the hierarchy even in Patler's absence, sent Matt Koehl (the party secretary) and a squad of stormtroopers to Patler’s residence . Their mission was to strip Patler of any remaining party property. Koehl’s group searched Patler’s room in an act designed to "add to Patler's humiliation" .

This event likely served as a psychological catalyst. Patler, who idolized Rockwell as a father figure, found himself rejected, humiliated, and impoverished by the very man he sought to emulate . In June 1967, an initial assassination attempt was made on Rockwell at his home. Shots were fired, but Rockwell survived unscathed. Although the perpetrator was not caught at the time, prosecutors would later argue this was Patler’s first failed attempt to exact revenge .

## 4\. The Assassination: August 25, 1967
### 4.1 The Setting: Dominion Hills
The Dominion Hills Shopping Center on Wilson Boulevard in Arlington was a typical suburban strip mall, featuring everyday conveniences like a laundromat, a barbershop, and a grocery store . It stood in stark contrast to the "barracks" located just across the street, creating a surreal proximity between domestic suburbia and radical extremism.

On Friday, August 25, 1967, the weather was typical for a Virginia summer. Rockwell, lacking a personal staff to handle domestic chores, was running errands. He drove his 1958 Chevrolet to the Econ-o-Wash laundromat at the shopping center .

### 4.2 The Timeline of the Shooting
The events of the assassination unfolded with rapid brutality just after noon.

| Time | Event | Details | Source |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **\~11:50 AM** | **Arrival** | Rockwell arrives at the Econ-o-Wash but realizes he forgot bleach. He tells the proprietor he must return home. | 1 |
| **\~12:00 PM** | **Return** | Rockwell returns to the laundromat with the bleach and loads his washing machine. | 1 |
| **12:02 PM** | **Departure** | Rockwell exits the laundromat and enters his vehicle. | 5 |
| **12:02 PM** | **The Shots** | Two shots are fired from the roof of the shopping center. | 1 |
| **12:03 PM** | **Impact** | Rockwell is struck in the chest and dies almost instantly. | 1 |
| **12:30 PM** | **Arrest** | John Patler is arrested at a bus stop on Washington Boulevard. | 1 |

### 4.3 The Mechanics of the Murder
As Rockwell slid into the front seat of his car, the assassin, positioned on the flat roof of the shopping center, took aim. The weapon used was a Mauser 7.63mm pistol, a German-manufactured semi-automatic firearm .

Two shots rang out. The first bullet smashed through the windshield of the Chevrolet. The second bullet found its mark, striking Rockwell in the chest and traversing his heart . The force of the impact and the sudden incapacitation caused Rockwell to lose control of his body; his foot likely slipped off the brake or hit the accelerator, causing the car to roll backward and collide with another vehicle in the lot .

Rockwell stumbled out of the passenger side door and collapsed onto the pavement. He landed face up, splayed beside a box of Ivory Snow detergent and a copy of the *New York Daily News*—a tableau of mundane consumer products surrounding the dying extremist . Bystanders, initially confused by the noise, rushed to the scene, but Rockwell died within minutes .

### 4.4 The Arrest
Witnesses at the shopping center immediately pointed police toward the roof and the direction of the fleeing gunman. Arlington police flooded the area. Approximately 30 minutes after the shooting, officers spotted a man fitting the suspect's description standing at a bus stop on Washington Boulevard, about a mile and a half from the crime scene .

The man was John Patler. He was sweating and out of breath. Police recovered the Mauser pistol, which had been discarded in a nearby creek bed or shrubbery along the escape route . Patler was taken into custody without incident.

## 5\. The Funeral Standoff: A Post-Mortem Political Crisis
The death of Rockwell did not end the spectacle; it merely transitioned it into a new phase involving the federal government. As a veteran who had been honorably discharged (prior to his political radicalization), Rockwell was legally entitled to burial in a National Cemetery . This created a dilemma for the U.S. government: how to fulfill the legal obligation to a veteran while preventing a Nazi demonstration on federal grounds.

### 5.1 The Army's Conditions
On August 27, 1967, the NSWPP announced that approval had been granted for Rockwell’s burial at Culpeper National Cemetery in Virginia . However, the Department of Defense, under the leadership of Secretary Robert McNamara, intervened with strict protocols. The Army specified that while Rockwell could be buried, no Nazi insignia, uniforms, flags, or armbands could be displayed within the confines of the cemetery .

The Pentagon was determined to prevent the National Cemetery from being used as a stage for political theater. General orders were issued to the military police guarding the cemetery to enforce this ban rigidly .

### 5.2 The Confrontation at Culpeper
On the morning of the funeral, a procession of over sixty vehicles departed Arlington for the 70-mile drive to Culpeper . The hearse carrying Rockwell was accompanied by party members, including Rockwell's successor Matt Koehl, who were dressed in full stormtrooper regalia—khaki shirts, swastika armbands, and combat boots .

When the procession arrived at the gates of Culpeper National Cemetery, they were met by a blockade of U.S. troops and military police . Helicopters circled overhead, bringing in reinforcements to ensure the standoff did not escalate into violence . The cemetery commander informed Koehl that they would not be permitted to enter unless they removed their Nazi insignia.

Koehl and the party leadership refused, viewing the removal of their uniforms as a betrayal of Rockwell’s ideology and an act of submission to the "Jewish-controlled" government . The standoff lasted for five hours . At one point, the hearse was stopped on the railroad tracks near the cemetery entrance and was nearly struck by an approaching train, adding a layer of chaotic danger to the stalemate .

### 5.3 Resolution and Cremation
With neither side willing to yield—the Army standing firm on federal regulations and the Nazis standing firm on their uniforms—the burial was aborted. The hearse turned around and returned the body to Arlington .

The following day, August 30, Rockwell’s body was secretly cremated . The disposition of his ashes became a subject of internal party mythos, with various factions later claiming possession. The confrontation at Culpeper resulted in a federal lawsuit, *Koehl v. Resor*, in which the Nazis sued Secretary of the Army Stanley Resor and Secretary of Defense Robert McNamara for violating their First Amendment rights . The courts ultimately upheld the government's right to regulate conduct and dress within National Cemeteries, ruling that the ban on political insignia was a content-neutral regulation of the facility .

## 6\. The Trial of John Patler: *Commonwealth v. Patler*
### 6.1 The Prosecution's Case
John Patler was indicted for first-degree murder and stood trial in the Circuit Court of Arlington County in late 1967\. The prosecution, led by Commonwealth’s Attorney Hassan, faced the challenge of a case that was largely circumstantial . There were no witnesses who could positively identify Patler's face as he pulled the trigger, only witnesses who saw a man of his general build fleeing the roof.

The prosecution built its case on a "web of evidence":

1. **Motive:** Prosecutors detailed the bitter schism between Patler and Rockwell, the expulsion, and the public humiliation Patler suffered . 
2. **The Weapon:** Ballistics experts linked the Mauser pistol found near the arrest site to the bullets that killed Rockwell. Crucially, prosecutors sought to prove Patler had possession of this weapon. They introduced evidence that the gun had been test-fired on a farm in Highland County owned by Patler's father-in-law . 
3. **Opportunity and Flight:** Patler was found fleeing the direction of the crime, sweating and out of breath, providing a timeline consistent with the shooter's escape .

### 6.2 The Defense and the "Open Fields" Doctrine
Patler’s defense team, led by attorney Thomas J. Harrigan, vigorously contested the admissibility of the evidence obtained from the father-in-law's farm. They argued that the police search of the farm to recover shell casings (used to match the murder weapon) was conducted without a warrant, violating Patler’s Fourth Amendment rights .

This legal argument centered on the "curtilage" vs. "open fields" distinction. The defense argued the farm was private property protected from warrantless search. However, the courts ruled that the protection of the Fourth Amendment extends only to the "curtilage" (the immediate area surrounding a dwelling) and not to open pastures or woods. The Virginia Supreme Court later affirmed this ruling in *Patler v. Commonwealth* (211 Va. 448), establishing a significant precedent in state law regarding the scope of police searches in rural areas .

### 6.3 Verdict and Sentencing
On December 15, 1967, after a trial that captivated the local community, the jury retired to deliberate. After only four hours, they returned with a guilty verdict for first-degree murder .

The sentencing phase resulted in a 20-year prison term . Legal analysts have noted that this sentence was relatively light for a premeditated political assassination, potentially reflecting the jury's view of the internal nature of the feud or the unsympathetic character of the victim.

### 6.4 Appeals and Parole
Patler appealed his conviction all the way to the U.S. Supreme Court. He was released on a $40,000 bond during the appellate process but was ordered back to prison in 1970 after the Virginia Supreme Court upheld his conviction . The U.S. Supreme Court denied his petition for certiorari in 1972 .

Patler served the majority of his sentence and was paroled in August 1975 . However, his entanglement with the legal system did not end there. In 1976, he violated the terms of his parole (citing trespassing and marijuana possession) and was returned to prison to serve an additional six years . Upon his final release, he changed his name back to John Patsalos and retreated into obscurity, reportedly disavowing the movement that had defined his early life .

## 7\. Sociological and Political Impact
### 7.1 The Decapitation of the Movement
The assassination of George Lincoln Rockwell demonstrated the fragility of personality-driven extremist movements. Rockwell *was* the party; his charisma, media savvy, and domineering personality held the disparate group of misfits together . His death created an immediate power vacuum that his successor, Matt Koehl, was ill-equipped to fill.

### 7.2 Succession and Fracturing
Matt Koehl, who assumed the title of Commander after the assassination, lacked Rockwell’s flair. Under his leadership, the NSWPP began to hemorrhage members. The movement fractured into several competing organizations, a process directly catalyzed by the loss of the unifying leader .

**Key Splinter Groups Post-Assassination:**

| Leader | Organization | Ideological Shift | Source |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Matt Koehl** | **NSWPP / The New Order** | Shifted toward "Esoteric Nazism," viewing Hitler as a spiritual entity; moved away from public political campaigning. | 6 |
| **William Pierce** | **National Alliance** | Former physics professor; focused on intellectualizing white supremacy; author of *The Turner Diaries*. | 6 |
| **Joseph Tommasi** | **NSLF** | Founded the National Socialist Liberation Front; advocated for immediate revolutionary violence and terrorism rather than political organizing. | 18 |
| **James Mason** | **Universal Order** | Influenced by the collapse; later advocated for *Siege* culture and leaderless resistance, inspired by Charles Manson. | 19 |

### 7.3 The Shift to "Esoteric" and Revolutionary Forms
Perhaps the most significant long-term consequence of the assassination was the shift in strategy within American neo-Nazism. Rockwell believed he could win through the American political system, predicting he would be elected president in 1972 . His death proved to many in the movement that the "system" would not protect them or allow them to succeed.

Consequently, the movement darkened. Koehl took the remnants of the party in a pseudo-religious direction, rebranding the NSWPP as "The New Order" in 1983 and focusing on the spiritual worship of Hitler . Others, like Tommasi and Pierce, abandoned the idea of winning elections entirely, turning instead to the concept of "leaderless resistance" and catastrophic revolutionary violence—a direct lineage to the domestic terror ideologies seen in later decades (e.g., The Order in the 1980s, Oklahoma City in 1995) .

## 8\. Conclusion
The assassination of George Lincoln Rockwell on August 25, 1967, was a violent resolution to the internal contradictions of the American Nazi Party. It was a crime born of the very hatred Rockwell cultivated—a hatred that eventually turned inward, pitting "pure" against "impure" within his own ranks.

While Rockwell failed to achieve the mass movement he envisioned, his murder profoundly altered the landscape of American extremism. It ended the era of the "media Nazi" who sought acceptance within the political mainstream and ushered in a fragmented, underground era of radicalization. The image of the slain Commander, lying in a parking lot next to a box of bleach, remains a potent symbol of the banal and brutal reality of political violence.

## 9\. Data and Statistics
### 9.1 Key Figures in the Case
| Name | Role | Outcome |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **George Lincoln Rockwell** | Victim / ANP Commander | Assassinated Aug 25, 1967\. |
| **John Patler** | Perpetrator / Former ANP Captain | Convicted of 1st Degree Murder; sentenced to 20 years. |
| **Matt Koehl** | Successor / Party Secretary | Assumed leadership; moved party to religious mysticism. |
| **Robert McNamara** | Secretary of Defense | Ordered the blockade of the funeral at Culpeper. |
| **Judge Charles S. Russell** | Presiding Judge | Oversaw *Commonwealth v. Patler*. |

### 9.2 Timeline of Legal Proceedings
| Date | Legal Event | Outcome |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Aug 25, 1967** | Arrest | Patler taken into custody. |
| **Dec 1967** | Trial | Jury trial in Arlington Circuit Court. |
| **Dec 15, 1967** | Verdict | Guilty of First Degree Murder. |
| **1970** | Appeal (*Patler v. Commonwealth*) | Virginia Supreme Court upholds conviction. |
| **1972** | Certiorari Denied | U.S. Supreme Court refuses to hear case. |
| **1975** | Parole | Patler released on parole. |
| **1976** | Re-incarceration | Patler violates parole; returns to prison. |

John Patler was indicted for first-degree murder and stood trial in the Circuit Court of Arlington County in late 1967.
The prosecution, led by Commonwealth’s Attorney Hassan, faced the challenge of a case that was largely circumstantial.
There were no witnesses who could positively identify Patler's face as he pulled the trigger, only witnesses who saw a man of his general build fleeing the roof.
The prosecution built its case on a "web of evidence" including motive, the weapon, and opportunity and flight.
Prosecutors detailed the bitter schism between Patler and Rockwell, the expulsion, and the public humiliation Patler suffered as motive.
Ballistics experts linked the Mauser pistol found near the arrest site to the bullets that killed Rockwell.
Crucially, prosecutors sought to prove Patler had possession of the murder weapon.
Prosecutors introduced evidence that the gun had been test-fired on a farm in Highland County owned by Patler's father-in-law.
John Patler was found fleeing the direction of the crime, sweating and out of breath, providing a timeline consistent with the shooter's escape.
Patler’s defense team, led by attorney Thomas J. Harrigan, vigorously contested the admissibility of the evidence obtained from the father-in-law's farm.
The defense argued that the police search of the farm to recover shell casings (used to match the murder weapon) was conducted without a warrant, violating Patler’s Fourth Amendment rights.
This legal argument centered on the "curtilage" vs. "open fields" distinction.
The defense argued the farm was private property protected from warrantless search.
The courts ruled that the protection of the Fourth Amendment extends only to the "curtilage" (the immediate area surrounding a dwelling) and not to open pastures or woods.

The Virginia Supreme Court later affirmed this ruling in *Patler v. Commonwealth* (211 Va. 448), establishing a significant precedent in state law regarding the scope of police searches in rural areas.
On December 15, 1967, after a trial that captivated the local community, the jury retired to deliberate.
After only four hours, the jury returned with a guilty verdict for first-degree murder.
The sentencing phase resulted in a 20-year prison term for John Patler.

Legal analysts have noted that this sentence was relatively light for a premeditated political assassination, potentially reflecting the jury's view of the internal nature of the feud or the unsympathetic character of the victim.
Patler appealed his conviction all the way to the U.S. Supreme Court.
John Patler was released on a $40,000 bond during the appellate process but was ordered back to prison in 1970 after the Virginia Supreme Court upheld his conviction.
The U.S. Supreme Court denied John Patler's petition for certiorari in 1972.
Patler served the majority of his sentence and was paroled in August 1975.
In 1976, John Patler violated the terms of his parole (citing trespassing and marijuana possession) and was returned to prison to serve an additional six years.
Upon his final release, John Patler changed his name back to John Patsalos and retreated into obscurity, reportedly disavowing the movement that had defined his early life.
The assassination of George Lincoln Rockwell demonstrated the fragility of personality-driven extremist movements.
Rockwell *was* the party; his charisma, media savvy, and domineering personality held the disparate group of misfits together.
Rockwell's death created an immediate power vacuum that his successor, Matt Koehl, was ill-equipped to fill.
Matt Koehl, who assumed the title of Commander after the assassination, lacked Rockwell’s flair.
Under Matt Koehl's leadership, the NSWPP began to hemorrhage members.
The movement fractured into several competing organizations, a process directly catalyzed by the loss of the unifying leader.
Matt Koehl led NSWPP / The New Order and shifted toward "Esoteric Nazism," viewing Hitler as a spiritual entity; moved away from public political campaigning.
William Pierce led National Alliance and focused on intellectualizing white supremacy; he was the author of *The Turner Diaries*.
Joseph Tommasi led NSLF and founded the National Socialist Liberation Front; advocated for immediate revolutionary violence and terrorism rather than political organizing.
James Mason led Universal Order and was influenced by the collapse; later advocated for *Siege* culture and leaderless resistance, inspired by Charles Manson.
Perhaps the most significant long-term consequence of the assassination was the shift in strategy within American neo-Nazism.
Rockwell believed he could win through the American political system, predicting he would be elected president in 1972.
Rockwell's death proved to many in the movement that the "system" would not protect them or allow them to succeed.
Consequently, the movement darkened.
Koehl took the remnants of the party in a pseudo-religious direction, rebranding the NSWPP as "The New Order" in 1983 and focusing on the spiritual worship of Hitler.

Others, like Tommasi and Pierce, abandoned the idea of winning elections entirely, turning instead to the concept of "leaderless resistance" and catastrophic revolutionary violence—a direct lineage to the domestic terror ideologies seen in later decades (e.g., The Order in the 1980s, Oklahoma City in 1995).
The assassination of George Lincoln Rockwell on August 25, 1967, was a violent resolution to the internal contradictions of the American Nazi Party.
The assassination of George Lincoln Rockwell was a crime born of the very hatred Rockwell cultivated—a hatred that eventually turned inward, pitting "pure" against "impure" within his own ranks.
While Rockwell failed to achieve the mass movement he envisioned, his murder profoundly altered the landscape of American extremism.
The assassination of George Lincoln Rockwell ended the era of the "media Nazi" who sought acceptance within the political mainstream and ushered in a fragmented, underground era of radicalization.
The image of the slain Commander, lying in a parking lot next to a box of bleach, remains a potent symbol of the banal and brutal reality of political violence.

“Barnum of the Bigots”
======================

[american history](https://www.press.uillinois.edu/wordpress/category/american-history/)[biography](https://www.press.uillinois.edu/wordpress/category/biography/)

[![Image 5: simonelli](http://www.press.uillinois.edu/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2016/07/simonelli.jpg)](http://www.press.uillinois.edu/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2016/07/simonelli.jpg)Not exactly the pride of Bloomington, Illinois, American Nazi leader George Lincoln Rockwell was born into—of all things—a family of vaudeville performers. A former associate shot him to death on August 25, 1967.

[Frederick Simonelli’s UIP biography of this powerful and enigmatic figure](http://www.press.uillinois.edu/books/catalog/84tdt4qt9780252022852.html) draws on primary sources of extraordinary depth, including declassified FBI files and manuscripts and other materials held by Rockwell’s family and associates. As Simonelli shows,Rockwell broadened his constituency beyond the Radical Right by articulating White Power politics in terms that were subsequently appropriated by the one-time Klansman David Duke. He also looks at how Rockwell’s influence remains potent almost fifty years after his assassination.The first objective assessment of the American Nazi party and an authoritative study of the roots of neo-nazism, neo-fascism, and White Power extremism in postwar America, _American Fuehrer_ is shocking and absorbing reading.

As Alex Haley memorably wrote in 1966, “Rockwell would have been first on any one’s list of those least likely to succeed as a racist demagogue or even to become one.” He had his failures, but his life had considerable successes, too. After a stint at Brown, he entered the U.S. Navy. He rose to the rank of commander, serving in World War II and the Korean War and earning plaudits for his skills as a pilot and officer. His second marriage, made while serving in Iceland, was conducted by the country’s Bishop in the National Cathedral. Once back in civilian life he won prizes for commercial art and by many accounts that career lay open to him.

But, ah, civilian life. That he was back in it at all hinted at the problem. In 1960, the Navy gave him an honorable discharge because… well, because during a period of naval service in San Diego, Rockwell became a virulent racist.

He founded the American Nazi Party in Arlington, Virginia. Thereafter he used a combination of marketing, provocation, and canny self-promotion to make himself one of the most recognizable fringe political figures in the nation’s history. ([His _Playboy_ magazine interview](https://archive.org/stream/1966PlayboyInterview/MicrosoftWord-Document1_djvu.txt) with Haley, the African American journalist and future _Roots_ icon, remains legendary.)

Rockwell was also one of the most influential of his ilk. Amidst the many marches and pamphlets and posing in his stormtrooper uniform, he gathered various strains of right-wing thought into a new religion called Christian Identity, a sect that found violent expression in the 1980s and 1990s. He all but mainstreamed Holocaust denial and internationalized the neo-Nazi movement. He even founded a record company that released white supremacist music, mastering an effective recruitment tool still used in the white power underground today.

5.title: Assassination of George Lincoln Rockwell
5.content:
| Assassination of George Lincoln Rockwell |
| --- |
| [![Image 1: People stand around Rockwell with a sheet over his body](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/99/George_Lincoln_Rockwell%2C_murdered%2C_with_a_sheet_over_his_body_%28cropped%29.png/330px-George_Lincoln_Rockwell%2C_murdered%2C_with_a_sheet_over_his_body_%28cropped%29.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:George_Lincoln_Rockwell,_murdered,_with_a_sheet_over_his_body_(cropped).png) The crime scene, Rockwell's body covered by a sheet |
| Location | [Arlington, Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arlington,_Virginia "Arlington, Virginia"), U.S. |
| Date | August 25, 1967; 58 years ago 12:02 p.m. |
| Attack type | Shooting |
| Weapon | [Mauser](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mauser "Mauser") pistol |
| Victim | [George Lincoln Rockwell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Lincoln_Rockwell "George Lincoln Rockwell") |
| Perpetrator | [John Patler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Patler "John Patler") |
| Motive | Revenge |
| Verdict | Guilty |
| Convictions | [First-degree murder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First-degree_murder "First-degree murder") |

On August 25, 1967, [George Lincoln Rockwell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Lincoln_Rockwell "George Lincoln Rockwell"), an American [neo-Nazi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neo-Nazi "Neo-Nazi") political activist and the leader of the [National Socialist White People's Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Socialist_White_People%27s_Party "National Socialist White People's Party") (NSWPP), formerly the American Nazi Party (ANP), was [assassinated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassinated "Assassinated") by [John Patler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Patler "John Patler"), an expelled member of the NSWPP. Patler fired two shots at Rockwell from the roof of a nearby building, while Rockwell was visiting a local laundromat close to the party's headquarters in [Arlington, Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arlington,_Virginia "Arlington, Virginia"). The second shot struck Rockwell in the chest; Rockwell died there at 12:02 p.m. Patler was arrested 45 minutes later, about a mile and a half away.

Rockwell was the founder of the ANP; he was one of the earliest [Holocaust deniers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holocaust_deniers "Holocaust deniers"), called for forcibly sending all [Black people](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_people "Black people") to [Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Africa "Africa"), and for the murder of [Jews](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jews "Jews"). Despite attention and widespread notoriety, neither Rockwell nor his party achieved political power and his following was largely insignificant. Rockwell had a complicated relationship with Patler, who left and rejoined the party several times. Patler was ultimately expelled in March 1967 for a variety of reasons, among them abandoning his post and causing dissension within the group's ranks. In June 1967, Rockwell was subject to an assassination attempt at his home. The perpetrator of this incident was not caught; prosecutors later alleged it to be Patler.

At trial, Patler was convicted of [first-degree murder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First-degree_murder "First-degree murder") and sentenced to 20 years in prison, of which he served 8. He was paroled, but was returned to prison after violating his parole. The evidence against Patler was [circumstantial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Circumstantial_evidence "Circumstantial evidence"), and Patler has never admitted guilt, though several legal appeals were all unsuccessful. The [funeral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Funeral "Funeral") itself was highly publicized, with a standoff between Rockwell's followers and authorities. During the resulting chaos, Rockwell's successor [Matt Koehl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Koehl "Matt Koehl") had Rockwell's body smuggled out of the funeral home and cremated.

Rockwell's death had a significant impact on the neo-Nazi movement, and Rockwell was seen as a [martyr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martyr "Martyr") by them. Though Rockwell was succeeded as group leader by Koehl, Koehl's leadership was poor and resulted in numerous schisms and people being driven from the party. Rockwell's death shocked the neo-Nazi movement, which as a whole decentralized after his death, and experienced large shifts in tactics and ideology. Many conspiracy theories emerged among Rockwell's followers, ranging from baseless allegations of a [Jewish conspiracy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jewish_conspiracy "Jewish conspiracy") to a coup by other high-ranking members of the NSWPP. Rockwell continues to be greatly influential on neo-Nazis.

### George Lincoln Rockwell and the American Nazi Party

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Assassination_of_George_Lincoln_Rockwell&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: George Lincoln Rockwell and the American Nazi Party")]

[![Image 2: Black and white profile shot of Rockwell with a corncob pipe in his mouth](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/61/GLR_with_massive_swastika_%28cropped%29.jpg/250px-GLR_with_massive_swastika_%28cropped%29.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:GLR_with_massive_swastika_(cropped).jpg)

Rockwell in 1965 at the ANP's headquarters

[George Lincoln Rockwell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Lincoln_Rockwell "George Lincoln Rockwell") was the founder and leader of the [American Nazi Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party "American Nazi Party"). He had founded the ANP in 1959, effectively the start of the neo-Nazi movement in the United States.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_George_Lincoln_Rockwell#cite_note-FOOTNOTESunshine202420%E2%80%9321-1) He called for gassing "Communist Jews" and forcibly deporting all [Black people](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_people "Black people") to [Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Africa "Africa");[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_George_Lincoln_Rockwell#cite_note-Miller2017-2) he was also one of the earliest [Holocaust deniers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holocaust_deniers "Holocaust deniers").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_George_Lincoln_Rockwell#cite_note-FOOTNOTENewton2014a479-3) A retrospective 2017 article from _[The Washington Post](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Washington\_Post "The Washington Post")_ said Rockwell was then "one of the most hated men in America".[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_George_Lincoln_Rockwell#cite_note-Miller2017-2) The party had only a few members, but garnered substantial media attention;[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_George_Lincoln_Rockwell#cite_note-FOOTNOTESunshine2024xix,_22-4) according to researcher [Spencer Sunshine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spencer_Sunshine "Spencer Sunshine"), though Rockwell was not the first American neo-Nazi, Rockwell "started the neo-Nazi movement in the United States as we know it."[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_George_Lincoln_Rockwell#cite_note-FOOTNOTESunshine202421-5) Scholar [William H. Schmaltz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_H._Schmaltz "William H. Schmaltz") wrote that Rockwell was the founder of an "Americanized version of National Socialism".[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_George_Lincoln_Rockwell#cite_note-FOOTNOTESunshine202422-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_George_Lincoln_Rockwell#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchmaltz2000XVII,_48-7)

Despite the attention and widespread notoriety, Rockwell and his party did not achieve political power and his following was largely insignificant.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_George_Lincoln_Rockwell#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWeir202438,_40-8) Rockwell ultimately came to recognize that a political movement solely devoted to provocation had limited real-world prospects, and so began to brainstorm new methods.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_George_Lincoln_Rockwell#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoodrick-Clarke200214-9) With it came a broader kind of racism, not just believing their audience to be Nordic or Germanic Whites, but Southern and Eastern Europeans, calling this "White Unity".[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_George_Lincoln_Rockwell#cite_note-Miller2017-2) In an effort to "de-Nazify" the party to increase its appeal to the masses,[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_George_Lincoln_Rockwell#cite_note-FOOTNOTESunshine202422-6) on January 1, 1967, the group underwent several changes, and was renamed to the National Socialist White People's Party (NSWPP). With the name change came a shift in the iconography to be more American.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_George_Lincoln_Rockwell#cite_note-FOOTNOTESimonelli19991-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_George_Lincoln_Rockwell#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchmaltz2000304-11)

In a June 1967 meeting, it was agreed that the party would shift away from the German National Socialist model, though the exact details of this meeting were later contested among those who attended.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_George_Lincoln_Rockwell#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKaplan2000b309%E2%80%93310-12) ANP second in command and "Hitler cultist" [Matt Koehl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Koehl "Matt Koehl") opposed all these changes,[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_George_Lincoln_Rockwell#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKaplan2000b309-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_George_Lincoln_Rockwell#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKaplan2000a155-14) as did [William Luther Pierce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Luther_Pierce "William Luther Pierce"), though Rockwell eventually prevailed.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_George_Lincoln_Rockwell#cite_note-FOOTNOTESimonelli1999102,_136-15) It may have been discussed that Koehl be replaced as second in command and successor by [Karl Allen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Allen "Karl Allen"), an estranged former member of the ANP, if Allen was brought back into the group. Several reconciliation meetings were held between Allen and Rockwell but Rockwell was assassinated before they could conclude.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_George_Lincoln_Rockwell#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKaplan2000b309-13) A week before Rockwell's death, the infant daughter of Rockwell and his mistress Barbara von Goetz died of a congenital illness, saddening him.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_George_Lincoln_Rockwell#cite_note-FOOTNOTESimonelli1999140-16)

[![Image 3: Black and white photo of Patler in uniform](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f6/John_Patler_in_the_Rockwell_Report_%28cropped%29.png/250px-John_Patler_in_the_Rockwell_Report_%28cropped%29.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:John_Patler_in_the_Rockwell_Report_(cropped).png)

Patler in 1963

Rockwell's eventual murderer was [John Patler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Patler "John Patler"), a member of the party, who helped produce Rockwell's propaganda as an editor for _[The Stormtrooper Magazine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Stormtrooper\_Magazine "The Stormtrooper Magazine")_.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_George_Lincoln_Rockwell#cite_note-FOOTNOTESimonelli1999101-17)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_George_Lincoln_Rockwell#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoodrick-Clarke200215-18) Patler was ethnically Greek, which led to criticism of his presence in the party by some neo-Nazis.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_George_Lincoln_Rockwell#cite_note-FOOTNOTESimonelli1999101-17) He changed his surname from Patsalos to Patler to make it sound more like Hitler.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_George_Lincoln_Rockwell#cite_note-Miller2017-2) Some other party members, mostly Pierce and Koehl, disliked him due to his Greek ethnic background and taunted him.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_George_Lincoln_Rockwell#cite_note-FOOTNOTESimonelli1999136-19) Rockwell liked Patler, whose presence he defended by arguing for the expanded idea of [master race](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Master_race "Master race") which included Greeks; "White" rather than the Nazi idea of "[Aryan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aryan_race "Aryan race")". Koehl and the members who agreed with him viewed this change as heretical.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_George_Lincoln_Rockwell#cite_note-FOOTNOTESunshine202422-6)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_George_Lincoln_Rockwell#cite_note-FOOTNOTESimonelli1999101%E2%80%93102-20) The changes to de-center the Nazism of the party and apply a broader base of racists that included Southern Europeans, including Greeks, were instigated by Patler.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_George_Lincoln_Rockwell#cite_note-Miller2017-2)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_George_Lincoln_Rockwell#cite_note-FOOTNOTESimonelli19991-10)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_George_Lincoln_Rockwell#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchmaltz2000305-21)

Patler was known to be unstable and had some [Marxist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marxist "Marxist") sympathies;[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_George_Lincoln_Rockwell#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoodrick-Clarke200215-18) he left the ANP in 1961 with [Dan Burros](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dan_Burros "Dan Burros") to form the American National Party, only to rejoin.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_George_Lincoln_Rockwell#cite_note-FOOTNOTENewton2014b160-22) Patler viewed Rockwell as a father figure but also blamed him for the problems in his life, and they began to conflict on several points.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_George_Lincoln_Rockwell#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchmaltz2000317-23)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_George_Lincoln_Rockwell#cite_note-FOOTNOTESimonelli1999135-24) From 1966 to 1967, Patler drifted in and out of the party.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_George_Lincoln_Rockwell#cite_note-FOOTNOTESimonelli1999135-24) Rockwell also had an affair with Patler's wife. Afterwards, Patler sent Rockwell a letter telling him he was fine with this.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_George_Lincoln_Rockwell#cite_note-FOOTNOTESimonelli1999136-19)[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_George_Lincoln_Rockwell#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWeir202447-25) Patler and his wife had two children together; after which he became more self-confident and questioned his position in the group. Hating the separation from his family, in March 1967, he left his post in [Spotsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spotsylvania_County,_Virginia "Spotsylvania County, Virginia") and returned to [Arlington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arlington_County,_Virginia "Arlington County, Virginia"). Rockwell then had the locks on his door cut off and Patler's possessions moved to Arlington.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_George_Lincoln_Rockwell#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchmaltz2000317-23)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_George_Lincoln_Rockwell#cite_note-FOOTNOTESimonelli1999134-26)

Afterwards, Rockwell wrote a discharge letter against Patler, including that he was guilty of "abandoning his post, gross insubordination and insulting conduct to superiors, neglect of duties, promotion of dissension among the ranks, promotion of distrust by non-Nordic members of the party, and usurpation of authority". Patler was then immediately dismissed.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_George_Lincoln_Rockwell#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoodrick-Clarke200215-18)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_George_Lincoln_Rockwell#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchmaltz2000317-23)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_George_Lincoln_Rockwell#cite_note-FOOTNOTENewton2014a160-27) Rockwell delegated this to Koehl instead of doing it himself. Patler spent the rest of the spring enraged over his treatment, writing letters disavowing Rockwell and the ANP, before again returning to begging for his forgiveness.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_George_Lincoln_Rockwell#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchmaltz2000305-21)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_George_Lincoln_Rockwell#cite_note-FOOTNOTESimonelli1999136-19) In his last letter to Rockwell, Patler wrote: "I don't think there are two people on earth who think and feel the same as we do. ... You are a very important part of my life. I need you as much as you need me. Without you there is no future".[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_George_Lincoln_Rockwell#cite_note-FOOTNOTESimonelli1999135%E2%80%93136-28)

### Prior assassination attempt

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Assassination_of_George_Lincoln_Rockwell&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Prior assassination attempt")]

Rockwell had been claiming for years that his enemies were stalking him,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_George_Lincoln_Rockwell#cite_note-Miller2017-2) and said for years that he believed he would be shot to death.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_George_Lincoln_Rockwell#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchmaltz2000326-29) Alan Welch, a member of the group, said that several months prior to the assassination, Rockwell had asked him to return to Arlington because he believed that someone was trying to kill him.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_George_Lincoln_Rockwell#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchmaltz2000326-29) On June 28, 1967, Rockwell was subject to a failed assassination attempt at his home. He found the party's headquarters' driveway to be blocked with a fallen tree and branches. When Rockwell went to clear it, a shot was fired, only narrowly missing his head.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_George_Lincoln_Rockwell#cite_note-FOOTNOTENewton2014a479-3)[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_George_Lincoln_Rockwell#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchmaltz2000320%E2%80%93321-30) Rockwell attempted to chase the shooter but he escaped, and Rockwell was unable to identify him.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_George_Lincoln_Rockwell#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchmaltz2000320%E2%80%93321-30)

Rockwell claimed that there had been two men.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_George_Lincoln_Rockwell#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchmaltz2000332-31) Rockwell's bodyguard Francis Joseph Smith claimed that afterwards, Rockwell told him he may have recognized one of the men, and that he "suspect[ed] treachery from someone very close to me" but that he did not want to say anything because, if he was wrong, it would irreparably damage the party.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_George_Lincoln_Rockwell#cite_note-FOOTNOTESimonelli1999138-32) Pierce said Rockwell told him there was actually only one man.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_George_Lincoln_Rockwell#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchmaltz2000332-31) After the murder and Patler's arrest, Hancock recounted witnessing this:[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_George_Lincoln_Rockwell#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchmaltz2000324%E2%80%93325-33)

> I saw a picture of the man they picked up on TV tonight, and I'm sure he's the one Rockwell and some other boy were chasing that day in June. I almost ran over him. I was in my car on Wilson Boulevard when Rockwell turned into his driveway, and I saw him and the boy with him dive out the door on the passenger's side and then run along Wilson Boulevard.... I turned into the street leading to my house, a man ran out of the bushes on one side, across the road, and into the bushes on the other side.... I had to step real hard on the brakes to avoid hitting him.

After this incident Rockwell contacted the police, and applied for a handgun carry permit two days later.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_George_Lincoln_Rockwell#cite_note-FOOTNOTENewton2014a479-3)[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_George_Lincoln_Rockwell#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchmaltz2000321-34) As of his death, the permit was pending.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_George_Lincoln_Rockwell#cite_note-FOOTNOTENewton2014a479-3) He also increased his security.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_George_Lincoln_Rockwell#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchmaltz2000321-34)

[![Image 4: Black and white photo of a car interior through an open car door, with a corncob pipe laying on the seat](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/59/Inside_of_Rockwell%27s_car_following_his_murder%2C_Associated_Press_wire_photo.png/250px-Inside_of_Rockwell%27s_car_following_his_murder%2C_Associated_Press_wire_photo.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Inside_of_Rockwell%27s_car_following_his_murder,_Associated_Press_wire_photo.png)

The inside of Rockwell's car following the assassination

On August 25, 1967, Rockwell woke up at 6:30 a.m. and had breakfast with other NSWPP members.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_George_Lincoln_Rockwell#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchmaltz2000322-35) The party planned to do an afternoon trip to [Washington, D.C.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington,_D.C. "Washington, D.C."), where they would distribute the premiere issue of _White Power_, the group's new newspaper.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_George_Lincoln_Rockwell#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchmaltz2000322-35) Rockwell worked on his book, _White Power_, which was published after his death.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_George_Lincoln_Rockwell#cite_note-Miller2017-2) Rockwell left the party's headquarters in Arlington, at 11:30 a.m. to do his laundry. He told the group members that he would be back shortly. The Speedy Laundromat was close to headquarters, just across Wilson Boulevard.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_George_Lincoln_Rockwell#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchmaltz2000322-35) He parked in front of the [laundromat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laundromat "Laundromat").[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_George_Lincoln_Rockwell#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchmaltz2000322-35)

After entering the laundromat, Rockwell told the attendant, Ruby Pierce, that he had forgotten something.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_George_Lincoln_Rockwell#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchmaltz2000322-35) His last words were that: "Oh, I forgot something";[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_George_Lincoln_Rockwell#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchmaltz2000322-35) the manager of the laundromat, John Hancock, said it had been [bleach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bleach "Bleach").[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_George_Lincoln_Rockwell#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchmaltz2000324-36) Returning to the car, Rockwell started it, backed out, and put it in drive.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_George_Lincoln_Rockwell#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchmaltz2000322-35) While Rockwell was in his car, two shots were fired through the driver's side windshield of his car.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_George_Lincoln_Rockwell#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchmaltz2000322-35) The shooter aimed from the laundromat's roof, which was flat and able to be stood on.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_George_Lincoln_Rockwell#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchmaltz2000322-35) The killer used a long-barrelled broomstick [Mauser](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mauser "Mauser") pistol. The first shot missed Rockwell, though hit his shirt, nicking the fabric, and instead hit the car's front seat.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_George_Lincoln_Rockwell#cite_note-FOOTNOTESimonelli19991-10)[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_George_Lincoln_Rockwell#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchmaltz2000322-35)

The second shot hit Rockwell in the chest and ruptured his [aorta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aorta "Aorta").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_George_Lincoln_Rockwell#cite_note-FOOTNOTESimonelli19991-10)[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_George_Lincoln_Rockwell#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchmaltz2000322,_327-37) The shot pushed Rockwell back against the car seat and knocked his [corncob pipe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corncob_pipe "Corncob pipe") out of his mouth.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_George_Lincoln_Rockwell#cite_note-FOOTNOTESimonelli19991-10)[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_George_Lincoln_Rockwell#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchmaltz2000322-35) The car, now with its driver incapacitated, rolled backwards and bumped another car, ending up at the other side of the lot.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_George_Lincoln_Rockwell#cite_note-FOOTNOTESimonelli19991-10)[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_George_Lincoln_Rockwell#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchmaltz2000322%E2%80%93323-38) Rockwell crawled into the passenger seat, opened the door from inside the car, and stepped out into the parking lot.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_George_Lincoln_Rockwell#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchmaltz2000322%E2%80%93323-38)[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_George_Lincoln_Rockwell#cite_note-FOOTNOTESimonelli19991%E2%80%932-39) It took Rockwell a minute or so to die.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_George_Lincoln_Rockwell#cite_note-FOOTNOTESimonelli19992-40) He rose to his feet, pointed to the roof the shooter had shot from, and turned to look at his headquarters. Rockwell's knees then buckled and he fell to the ground.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_George_Lincoln_Rockwell#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchmaltz2000322%E2%80%93323-38)[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_George_Lincoln_Rockwell#cite_note-FOOTNOTESimonelli19991%E2%80%932-39) Rockwell died there at 12:02 p.m,[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_George_Lincoln_Rockwell#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchmaltz2000322%E2%80%93323-38)[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_George_Lincoln_Rockwell#cite_note-FOOTNOTESimonelli19992-40) death resulting from massive hemorrhaging resulting from damage to the blood vessels.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_George_Lincoln_Rockwell#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchmaltz2000327-41)

The killing made headline news internationally and resulted in a wide amount of notoriety.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_George_Lincoln_Rockwell#cite_note-Miller2017-2) The news cycle continued for over a week, especially given what occurred at the funeral.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_George_Lincoln_Rockwell#cite_note-Miller2017-2) Rockwell's estranged father, the former vaudeville actor [George Lovejoy Rockwell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Lovejoy_Rockwell "George Lovejoy Rockwell"), said of his son's murder that: "I'm not surprised at all. I've expected it for quite some time. I think he would have liked to have gotten rid of the whole Nazi mess. He was more afraid of his own men than people were of him."[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_George_Lincoln_Rockwell#cite_note-Woodard2017-42)[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_George_Lincoln_Rockwell#cite_note-Chicago_Tribune1967-43) He also said that to him, it seemed like his son had had a sort of premonition of his own death.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_George_Lincoln_Rockwell#cite_note-Chicago_Tribune1967-43) The mayor of New York City, [John Lindsay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Lindsay "John Lindsay"), said that the killing evidenced "violence breeds violence and extremism breeds extremism", and advocated for increased gun control.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_George_Lincoln_Rockwell#cite_note-The_Cincinnati_Enquirer1967-44)

The Jewish community had a generally mixed response. In the aftermath, many Jewish figures and organizations spoke out against violence and for [gun control](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gun_control "Gun control") while denouncing Rockwell's beliefs.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_George_Lincoln_Rockwell#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchmaltz2000326-29)[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_George_Lincoln_Rockwell#cite_note-The_Cincinnati_Enquirer1967-44) Journalist [Harry Golden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Golden "Harry Golden") called the murder deplorable,[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_George_Lincoln_Rockwell#cite_note-The_Cincinnati_Enquirer1967-44) and Samuel Samuels, the leader of the [Jewish War Veterans of the United States of America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jewish_War_Veterans_of_the_United_States_of_America "Jewish War Veterans of the United States of America"), said the killer "has done a great disservice to the nation in the elimination of Rockwell by making a martyr of a despicable enemy of America."[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_George_Lincoln_Rockwell#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchmaltz2000326-29)[Arthur Lelyveld](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_Lelyveld "Arthur Lelyveld"), the president of the [American Jewish Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Jewish_Congress "American Jewish Congress"), called Rockwell "a nuisance rather than a menace to American institutions", but said that the AJC "condemn the use of violence, even when it is directed against the enemies of democracy".[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_George_Lincoln_Rockwell#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchmaltz2000326-29)[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_George_Lincoln_Rockwell#cite_note-The_Cincinnati_Enquirer1967-44)[Ted Weiss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ted_Weiss "Ted Weiss"), commented that he abhorred Rockwell's views but that "this violence has no political discrimination. [...] It hits left and the right, the young and the old. This carnage has to be controlled. How much longer do we go on killing people senselessly?"[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_George_Lincoln_Rockwell#cite_note-The_Cincinnati_Enquirer1967-44)[Benjamin Epstein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benjamin_Epstein "Benjamin Epstein") of the [Anti-Defamation League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anti-Defamation_League "Anti-Defamation League") stated that the ADL, one of Rockwell's "prime targets, hopes his killer will be brought to justice", but that it was "ironic that a man who for so long advocated and incited violence and trained his followers in the use of firearms, should himself reach a violent end".[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_George_Lincoln_Rockwell#cite_note-The_Cincinnati_Enquirer1967-44)

Among neo-Nazis nationally and internationally, the reaction was largely one of shock and disbelief.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_George_Lincoln_Rockwell#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKaplan2000a357%E2%80%93358-45) Swedish neo-Nazi [Göran Assar Oredsson](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=G%C3%B6ran_Assar_Oredsson&action=edit&redlink=1 "Göran Assar Oredsson (page does not exist)")([sv](https://sv.wikipedia.org/wiki/G%C3%B6ran_Assar_Oredsson "sv:Göran Assar Oredsson")), the leader of [The Nordic Realm Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nordic_Realm_Party "The Nordic Realm Party") and a friend of Rockwell, was distraught.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_George_Lincoln_Rockwell#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKaplan2000a358-46) British neo-Nazi [Colin In a 2000 study of public perception of various high profile assassinations in the _[Public Opinion Quarterly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public\_Opinion\_Quarterly "Public Opinion Quarterly")_, 49% of people said they were "not surprised" by Rockwell's assassination, compared to 31% for the [assassination of Martin Luther King Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_Martin_Luther_King_Jr. "Assassination of Martin Luther King Jr.") and 3% and 8% for the [assassination of John F. Kennedy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_John_F._Kennedy "Assassination of John F. Kennedy") and [Robert F.
