| [Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_party "Political party") | [American Nazi Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party "American Nazi Party") |
| [Alma mater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alma_mater "Alma mater") | [University of Wisconsin–Milwaukee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Wisconsin%E2%80%93Milwaukee "University of Wisconsin–Milwaukee") |
|  |

**Matthias Koehl Jr.** (January 22, 1935 – October 9/10, 2014) was an American [neo-Nazi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neo-Nazi "Neo-Nazi") politician and religious leader who served as the second leader of the [American Nazi Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party "American Nazi Party") from 1967 to 2014. He joined the party in 1960 following membership in various [white supremacist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_supremacist "White supremacist") groups, and succeeded to leadership following [the assassination](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_George_Lincoln_Rockwell "Assassination of George Lincoln Rockwell") of the founder of the party, [George Lincoln Rockwell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Lincoln_Rockwell "George Lincoln Rockwell"), in 1967.

Koehl became unpopular in the movement, alienating the party's members and attempting to consolidate power by removing his opposition from the party; often those cut off went on to form opposition groups. Koehl was very concerned with his unpopular image and made alliances with worldwide neo-fascists such as [Hans-Ulrich Rudel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans-Ulrich_Rudel "Hans-Ulrich Rudel") and [Povl Riis-Knudsen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Povl_Riis-Knudsen "Povl Riis-Knudsen"). Koehl cut down on the organisation's previous publicity stunts under Rockwell.

In 1983, Koehl renamed the organization the New Order and transformed it into a religious organization, influenced by the fascist writer [Savitri Devi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Savitri_Devi "Savitri Devi"). The New Order promoted occult veneration of [Adolf Hitler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adolf_Hitler "Adolf Hitler") as an avatar of God. Eventually in 1985 the group came under financial troubles and relocated from Washington DC to Wisconsin and Michigan. Koehl revealed little personal information to the group's members, who were low in number but sturdy. Koehl died in 2014, aged 79, and was succeeded by [Martin Kerr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Kerr "Martin Kerr").

Koehl was born on January 22, 1935 in [Milwaukee, Wisconsin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milwaukee,_Wisconsin "Milwaukee, Wisconsin") to [Hungarian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungarians "Hungarians") immigrants of [German](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germans_in_Hungary "Germans in Hungary") descent.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Koehl#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoodrick-Clarke200215-1) Koehl's father, Matthias Koehl Sr., claimed that his son rarely spoke with him about personal matters, but "was more talkative to his mother".[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Koehl#cite_note-DailyTelegram1967-2) At a young age, Koehl had a reputation for being vocally antisemitic.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Koehl#cite_note-FOOTNOTESimonelli199977%E2%80%9379-3) Koehl first professed admiration for Hitler at age 13[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Koehl#cite_note-FOOTNOTENewton2014157-4) and disrupted a school lesson by defending the German dictator.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Koehl#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBornstein198664-5) He distributed racist literature at his high school and served as a spokesman for the Nazi group the American Action Army.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Koehl#cite_note-FOOTNOTENewton2014157-4)

He graduated from a high school in his home town in 1952,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Koehl#cite_note-DailyTelegram1967-2) and became the leader of the young guard of the [National Renaissance Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Renaissance_Party_(United_States) "National Renaissance Party (United States)").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Koehl#cite_note-FOOTNOTENewton2014157-4) He then moved to Chicago, where he worked as an encyclopedia salesman,[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Koehl#cite_note-FOOTNOTENewton2014157-4)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Koehl#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAtkins2002160-6) before he went to the [University of Wisconsin–Milwaukee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Wisconsin%E2%80%93Milwaukee "University of Wisconsin–Milwaukee") to study journalism.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Koehl#cite_note-DailyTelegram1967-2) There, he played the violin alongside the civic opera.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Koehl#cite_note-MilwaukeeMagazine2008-7) He subsequently enlisted in the [United States Marine Corps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Marine_Corps "United States Marine Corps") and spent two years under them.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Koehl#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoodrick-Clarke200215-1)

[![Image 3: Black-and-white photo Koehl holding an American flag](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8a/Matthias_Koehl.jpg/250px-Matthias_Koehl.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Matthias_Koehl.jpg)

Koehl, pictured at a National Renaissance Party rally in 1953

In 1956, Koehl visited the "We the People" convention at the [La Salle Hotel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Salle_Hotel "La Salle Hotel"), where he was told by a member of the [Sons of the American Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sons_of_the_American_Revolution "Sons of the American Revolution") about [George Lincoln Rockwell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Lincoln_Rockwell "George Lincoln Rockwell")'s plans to form a Nazi party. Koehl was initially shocked by the concept, but hoped it was legitimate.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Koehl#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchmaltz2000101-8)

Koehl subsequently moved between various white supremacist parties. He helped with the organization of the [United White Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=United_White_Party&action=edit&redlink=1 "United White Party (page does not exist)"),[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Koehl#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoodrick-Clarke200215-1) and visited its founding meeting.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Koehl#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchmaltz2000101-8) Koehl became the national organizer of the [National States' Rights Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_States%27_Rights_Party "National States' Rights Party"),[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Koehl#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoodrick-Clarke200215-1) where he first met Rockwell in 1958;[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Koehl#cite_note-FOOTNOTESimonelli199977%E2%80%9379-3) they worked on [John G. Crommelin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_G._Crommelin "John G. Crommelin")'s campaign.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Koehl#cite_note-SPLC2014-9) By 1959, he was a member of the Fighting American Nationalists, a front group for Rockwell's [American Nazi Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party "American Nazi Party") (ANP),[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Koehl#cite_note-FOOTNOTENewton2014157-4) before he joined the ANP proper in 1960.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Koehl#cite_note-SPLC2014-9) According to author [Frederick J. Simonelli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_J._Simonelli "Frederick J. Simonelli"), Koehl and Rockwell became close friends after meeting, as Rockwell's extreme personality complimented Koehl's introverted nature. Simonelli compared this to the relationship between [Adolf Hitler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adolf_Hitler "Adolf Hitler") and [Martin Bormann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Bormann "Martin Bormann").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Koehl#cite_note-FOOTNOTESimonelli199977%E2%80%9379-3)

In the 1950s, Koehl was roommates with [Eustace Mullins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eustace_Mullins "Eustace Mullins"), and the two visited [St. Elizabeths Hospital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Elizabeths_Hospital "St. Elizabeths Hospital") in order to meet poet and fascist collaborator [Ezra Pound](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ezra_Pound "Ezra Pound").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Koehl#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFeldmanRinaldi201450-10) Later, during Koehl's leadership of the ANP, Pound's poetry was reprinted in the group's journal,[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Koehl#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFeldmanRinaldi201451-11) and he was associated with the Committee to Free Ezra Pound in the 1950s.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Koehl#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOakley198776-12)

### With the American Nazi Party

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Matt_Koehl&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: With the American Nazi Party")]

[![Image 4: Colonel Francisco Caamaño Deño, the man who was president of the Dominican Republic, is wearing a short-sleeved button-up shirt, and a necktie](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/bc/Koehl_1967_%28cropped%29.jpg/250px-Koehl_1967_%28cropped%29.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Koehl_1967_(cropped).jpg)

[![Image 5: Man in a suit with a tie poses for a photo](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/33/George_Lincoln_Rockwell_at_WMU%2C_1967.jpg/120px-George_Lincoln_Rockwell_at_WMU%2C_1967.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:George_Lincoln_Rockwell_at_WMU,_1967.jpg)

Koehl and Rockwell c. 1967

Koehl left the National States' Rights Party to become the leader of the Chicago division of the ANP[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Koehl#cite_note-FOOTNOTENewton2014157-4) in 1961, then moved to Rockwell's headquarters in 1963. This promotion of location accompanied his promotion to corresponding secretary of the [World Union of National Socialists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Union_of_National_Socialists "World Union of National Socialists") and national secretary of the ANP; in addition, he edited and published bulletins for both groups.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Koehl#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoodrick-Clarke200215-1) By late 1963, he had been promoted to major and national secretary, the chief administrative officer, ending the vacancy left by [James K. Warner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_K._Warner "James K. Warner"),[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Koehl#cite_note-FOOTNOTESimonelli199977%E2%80%9379-3) and by 1966, he was deputy commander in the aftermath of the resignation of Alan Welch.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Koehl#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKaplan2000154%E2%80%93155-13)

One frequent rumor that plagued Koehl during his period under Rockwell was accusations that he was a homosexual.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Koehl#cite_note-FOOTNOTESimonelli199977%E2%80%9379-3)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Koehl#cite_note-FOOTNOTESunshine202458-14) Allegations included that in 1951, when he was 16 years old, he had sexual relations with two older male members of the Committee to Free Ezra Pound, or that he, alongside those two members, sexually assaulted a 15-year-old boy.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Koehl#cite_note-FOOTNOTESimonelli199977%E2%80%9379-3) Rick Cooper, leader of the [National Socialist Vanguard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Socialist_Vanguard "National Socialist Vanguard"), claimed that he found Koehl engaged in sex with a man in 1958,[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Koehl#cite_note-FOOTNOTESimonelli199977%E2%80%9379-3) and [James Mason](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Mason_(neo-Nazi) "James Mason (neo-Nazi)") spread evidence-less booklets alleging that he was gay.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Koehl#cite_note-FOOTNOTESunshine202429-15) There was no proof of such allegations, but it deeply affected Rockwell, who attempted to "prove" Koehl's heterosexuality by trying to marry him to a Nazi woman. However, she did not appeal to Koehl, who ignored her.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Koehl#cite_note-FOOTNOTESimonelli199977%E2%80%9379-3)

Koehl clashed with Rockwell.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Koehl#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBerry201748-16)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Koehl#cite_note-FOOTNOTESimonelli1995561-17) In August 1966, Rockwell angrily rejected a suggestion from Koehl that they should have more staff (at the time, the ANP did not have enough money for food and could not pay for new employees).[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Koehl#cite_note-FOOTNOTESimonelli1995561-17) On August 24th, 1967, Rockwell and Koehl had another verbal dispute; an "acrimonious showdown" according to Rockwell biography Frederick Simonelli, where an eyewitness reported that Rockwell claimed Koehl would be expelled from the Party. The following day, Rockwell [was assassinated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_George_Lincoln_Rockwell "Assassination of George Lincoln Rockwell").[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Koehl#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBerry201748-16)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Koehl#cite_note-FOOTNOTESimonelli1999136%E2%80%93137-18) While due to the argument there was speculation Koehl may have been involved (a theory supported by various people who knew Rockwell, including his lover Barbara von Goetz), the man convicted for the assassination was a former ANP member named [John Patler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Patler "John Patler").[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Koehl#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBerry201748-16)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Koehl#cite_note-FOOTNOTESimonelli1999136%E2%80%93137-18) Despite the conviction, dissident Nazis spread posters stating that Koehl was wanted for Rockwell's murder.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Koehl#cite_note-FOOTNOTENewton2014157-4)

During Patler's time in the Party, he had hated Koehl for their disagreements on race; Patler, who was ethnically Greek, supported Rockwell's pan-white supremacy, while Koehl cared only for "Nordic" whites, and was uncomfortable with Patler's presence in the group.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Koehl#cite_note-FOOTNOTESimonelli1999136%E2%80%93137-18) Rockwell and Patler had repeatedly argued and subsequently reconciled prior to Patler being forced out of the Party by Rockwell in March 1967. Rockwell sent Koehl to deliver the order, and Koehl brought ANP stormtroopers to search Patler's room and stop him from stealing Party property to "[add] to Patler's humiliation," according to Simonelli.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Koehl#cite_note-FOOTNOTESimonelli1999136%E2%80%93137-18) At the time, Koehl claimed to newsmen the party "[didn't] know of anyone who [could] fill [Rockwell's] shoes",[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Koehl#cite_note-19) but Koehl was selected as leader by a group of 16 Party members[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Koehl#cite_note-:0-20) and succeeded Rockwell as commander of the National Socialist White People's Party, the-at-the-time name of the American Nazi Party.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Koehl#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoodrick-Clarke200215-1)

[![Image 6: A man in a suit stands sternly in front of an American flag and a Nazi flag, with two men in the background](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/22/Matthias_Koehl_%26_the_American_Nazi_Party_%28cropped%29.jpg/250px-Matthias_Koehl_%26_the_American_Nazi_Party_%28cropped%29.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Matthias_Koehl_%26_the_American_Nazi_Party_(cropped).jpg)

Koehl with other ANP members in 1967

Immediately after Rockwell's death, groups like the [American Jewish Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Jewish_Committee "American Jewish Committee") believed he would be incapable of keeping the loyalty of the Nazis, believing him not as charismatic as Rockwell. This prediction proved to hold weight, as soon after achieving the position, Koehl became unpopular.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Koehl#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBornstein198665-21) His style of leadership alienated old members and made many new members leave.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Koehl#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKaplan2000155%E2%80%93156-22) Shortly after Koehl gained power, two other high-ranking members of the Party, Robert Lloyd and [William Luther Pierce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Luther_Pierce "William Luther Pierce"), requested that he share power between the three of them. Koehl responded distastefully and Pierce was forced to leave the organization. Future [Atomwaffen Division](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomwaffen_Division "Atomwaffen Division") advisor [James Mason](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Mason_(neo-Nazi) "James Mason (neo-Nazi)") lost faith in Koehl's leadership because of the incident, but stayed in the organization because he "didn't know what else to do".[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Koehl#cite_note-FOOTNOTESunshine202425-23) Many former members of the group were purged of their positions in Koehl's attempt to compose the Party of people completely loyal to him. He took control of the World Union of National Socialists (WUNS), and his leadership there was also criticized.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Koehl#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKaplan2000155%E2%80%93156-22)

Koehl suspended [Joseph Tommasi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Tommasi "Joseph Tommasi"), a California-based Party member, and soon after the group's Cleveland organizer, Casey Kalemba, left; both formed their own Neo-Nazi groups outside of the ANP.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Koehl#cite_note-FOOTNOTESunshine202426-24) An article in _[The Record Herald](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Record\_Herald "The Record Herald")_ claimed he lacked the way Rockwell carried himself and commanded respect.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Koehl#cite_note-RecordHerald1968-25) Similarly an article in the [American Jewish Year Book](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Jewish_Year_Book "American Jewish Year Book") stated these splits were due to Koehl lacking Rockwell's leadership ability; a few units, example including the division in Los Angeles, split off from the Party rather than following him.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Koehl#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEllerin1968269-26) Koehl was criticized by loyalists of Rockwell like Robert Surrey,[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Koehl#cite_note-FOOTNOTESimonelli199941-27) and former members of the party, like [Harold Covington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harold_Covington "Harold Covington"), actively pushed for Koehl to be overthrown in his leadership.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Koehl#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKaplan2000155-28) James Mason called him an "orthodox, cultist [conservative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservatism_and_fascism "Conservatism and fascism")" with "no talent" and "no charisma".[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Koehl#cite_note-FOOTNOTESunshine202429-15) Nonetheless this lack of trust in Koehl was not universal, and the Party remained strong for years following Pierce leaving. Koehl was praised by Australian nationalist [Jim Saleam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jim_Saleam "Jim Saleam") as "[standing] above his contemporaries", claiming his ideas "appear to be the basis of American Nazi thinking".[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Koehl#cite_note-FOOTNOTESunshine202426-24)

In an attempt to disperse this view of him, Koehl traveled to [West Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Germany "West Germany") and had his photograph taken with several former members of the original Nazi Party, publishing many of the images, chief among them one in which he shook hands with Nazi military officer [Hans-Ulrich Rudel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans-Ulrich_Rudel "Hans-Ulrich Rudel").[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Koehl#cite_note-FOOTNOTELee1999165%E2%80%93166-29) These photographs were published alongside photos of people he had shaken hands with doing the same with Hitler, suggesting a connection between the leader of the Third Reich and Koehl. Another attempt to boost his opinion amongst extremists was his alliance with Danish Nazi leader [Povl Riis-Knudsen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Povl_Riis-Knudsen "Povl Riis-Knudsen"), who became General Secretary of the WUNS.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Koehl#cite_note-FOOTNOTELee1999165%E2%80%93166-29)

During Koehl's leadership of the group, they backed away from their attacks on other racial groups to instead focus on "positive" aspects of the Neo-Nazi ideology.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Koehl#cite_note-SPLC2014-9) He consolidated the Party, shutting down the California and Chicago units,[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Koehl#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchmaltz2000335-30) and largely stopped the organization from pursuing the publicity stunts they under Rockwell were known for. Instead, the message was spread primarily through prerecorded messages from Koehl sent to telephones, urging the receiver to follow the "White Power message"; one example being his request that people in [Washington, D.C.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington,_D.C. "Washington, D.C.") disobey the gun control laws and keep at least 100 rounds for every weapon they own.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Koehl#cite_note-RecordHerald1968-25) One plot Koehl's party became known for during the 1980s were "Victory Bonds", a scheme mimicking [War bonds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_bond "War bond") where money invested would be given back once Koehl achieved power. The [U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Securities_and_Exchange_Commission "U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission") shut down Victory Bonds after they became aware of it in a failed suit from Rick Cooper to get his money back.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Koehl#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKaplan2000157-31)

Koehl came to believe that "all the problems [faced] in North America are fundamentally spiritual in origin", and claimed that Hitler said at the end of his life that Nazism could be revived "as a religious movement". He came to believe that the Party was inherently religious, and should stop attempting to pursue politics. Therefore,[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Koehl#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGardell200384%E2%80%9385-32) in 1983, Koehl renamed the organization the [New Order](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Order_(Neo-Nazi_group) "New Order (Neo-Nazi group)") and made it more overtly religious, espousing that Hitler had been sent down to Earth by a divine entity, reflecting his inspiration from fascist author [Savitri Devi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Savitri_Devi "Savitri Devi").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Koehl#cite_note-SPLC2014-9) He wrote in 1993 that the New Order was the only group dedicated "totally, exclusively, uncompromisingly and without reservation to the Cause of Adolf Hitler,"[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Koehl#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAtkins201194-33) and the front page of the New Order's website describes it as "a faith in the fullest sense of the word" and "a religion".[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Koehl#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFeldmanRinaldi201450-10) This near-cult of Hitler was what led Povl Riis-Knudsen to become disillusioned with Koehl and his group.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Koehl#cite_note-FOOTNOTELee1999166-34)

By the early 1980s, the organization's membership was dwindling, and groups like the Chico Area National Socialists were still splitting off. Koehl sought out a policy, inconsistent with previous traditions, of collaborating with other organizations; a "practical demonstration of [white unity]" as he described it. However, this failed, as differences both personal and in beliefs split the groups apart.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Koehl#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGeorgeWilcox1997331-35) He and the Order came under heavy financial troubles in the 1980s from both the [Internal Revenue Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internal_Revenue_Service "Internal Revenue Service")[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Koehl#cite_note-SPLC2014-9) (who had given him and his group a [lien](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lien "Lien") for $37,000 in unpaid taxes)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Koehl#cite_note-FOOTNOTENewton2014157-4) and the cost of living in Washington, D.C., which culminated in him dispersing the Order to Wisconsin and Michigan[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Koehl#cite_note-SPLC2014-9) in 1985.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Koehl#cite_note-:0-20) The [Anti-Defamation League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anti-Defamation_League "Anti-Defamation League") estimated in 1984 that the New Order had only 25 hardcore members and roughly 100 followers, and by 1997 it was considered tiny in membership and unusually stable for a hate group.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Koehl#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGeorgeWilcox1997331-35) Koehl stayed very secretive and followers knew little about him, but were completely trusting of him. Koehl kept himself locked in his office for most of the day then went home—members of the organization were not told what he did afterwards or the location of where he lived.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Koehl#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOakley198776-12) Public demonstrations of the organization were rare, and never numbered more than twenty people; annual income estimates were under $100,000.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Koehl#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBornstein198667-36)

Koehl opposed the trend of [White power skinheads](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_power_skinhead "White power skinhead") and attacked [David Duke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Duke "David Duke")'s "repudiation of all things Nazi" during the [1991 Louisiana gubernatorial election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1991_Louisiana_gubernatorial_election "1991 Louisiana gubernatorial election"). He missed opportunities to gain support for the New Order, and lived in obscurity from then on.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Koehl#cite_note-:0-20) By 1992, the World Union of National Socialists no longer held significant power over the movement, and was formally restructured into a policy-making group over a membership-based organization. Rockwell and British Nazi leader [Colin Jordan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colin_Jordan "Colin Jordan")'s vision for the WUNS as a firmly structured group never came to fruition.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Koehl#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchmaltz2000338-37)

Koehl died in the night between October 9 and 10, 2014, at the age of 79. His death was reported by the New Order in a short statement, and then by the [Southern Poverty Law Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Poverty_Law_Center "Southern Poverty Law Center").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Koehl#cite_note-SPLC2014-9) He was succeeded as leader of the New Order by [Martin Kerr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Kerr "Martin Kerr").[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Koehl#cite_note-Murphy2018-38)

Ideology and beliefs
--------------------

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Matt_Koehl&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Ideology and beliefs")]

Koehl was an obsessive adherent to classic German Nazism and admired Adolf Hitler, being strongly antisemitic.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Koehl#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKaplan2000154-39) Even from his entrance into the ANP, Koehl was interested in joining the group because of his great respect for the German Führer. While writing for _[National Socialist World](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National\_Socialist\_World "National Socialist World")_, he depicted him as a visionary ideological thinker with more roots in [White nationalism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_nationalism "White nationalism") than [German nationalism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_nationalism "German nationalism"), and thought of Nazism as a new faith. He saw the ideology not as pushing for something political or social, but for a "universal transformation of ideas and things."[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Koehl#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoodrick-Clarke200215%E2%80%9316-40) Koehl was, according to Simonelli, a "rabid germanophile" who opposed the removal of the swastika from the group's image by Rockwell.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Koehl#cite_note-FOOTNOTESimonelli19991-41)

In an [Associated Press](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Associated_Press "Associated Press") interview from after he took power, Koehl claimed he had been "born a racist", opposed [miscegenation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miscegenation "Miscegenation"), and believed in the establishment of an "all-white America". He went on to say that [race war](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Class_conflict "Class conflict") was "just around the corner." He pushed to first build up the Party within, constructing a "revolutionary cadre", and then to form a "[Grassroots movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grassroots_movement "Grassroots movement") in American politics".[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Koehl#cite_note-RecordHerald1968-25) Koehl said that he wished to "send [African-Americans] [back to Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Back_to_Africa "Back to Africa")", and that those who did not go of their own will should be forced to or killed.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Koehl#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDavis199810-42) Years later he claimed again that "Blacks are the pawns of the Jews", and that he had nothing against Black people inherently, but thought miscegenation was a form of genocide and that [White separatism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_separatism "White separatism") was the only way to "build the White race strong again". [[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Koehl#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDavis199811%E2%80%9312-43) He said in a 1976 _[Crawdaddy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crawdaddy\_(magazine) "Crawdaddy (magazine)")_ interview that it was "a mistake" for colonists to bring Africans into the United States, and elaborated on his views on Jewish people; he believed that there would be none in his ideal society, and that a potential solution was to bring them to "a big island somewhere in the middle of the Ocean" where they could "perform hard and honest work", continuing that "if it kills them… it is their tough luck".[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Koehl#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGeorgeWilcox1997331-35)

Koehl further developed his admiration of Hitler by reforming the party into the New Order.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Koehl#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoodrick-Clarke200216-44) In this group, Koehl implemented religious elements, imaging it as a faithful community.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Koehl#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGardell200384-45) In the book _[Black Sun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black\_Sun\_(Goodrick-Clarke\_book) "Black Sun (Goodrick-Clarke book)")_, [Nicholas Goodrick-Clarke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicholas_Goodrick-Clarke "Nicholas Goodrick-Clarke") emphasizes the extents to which the organization's discussion of Hitler was religious; the New Order produced literature praising him in a manner Goodrick-Clarke considered to be imitative of [Jesus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jesus "Jesus"), Koehl himself directly compared the cause and followers of Hitler to that of the Christian messiah in a 1991 speech to European members of the New Order,[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Koehl#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoodrick-Clarke200216%E2%80%9317-46) and, while talking about Rockwell after his death, compared his role within the Nazi ideology to that of [St. Paul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_the_Apostle "Paul the Apostle") within Christianity.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Koehl#cite_note-FOOTNOTESimonelli1999122-47) Koehl made claims that Hitler was "a gift of Almighty Providence" and that by rejecting him, "we rejected God himself".[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Koehl#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGardell200384%E2%80%9385-32) He claimed in 1985 that Hitler had "risen from the grave",[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Koehl#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGardell200385-48) and described him as the "greatest figure to ever walk the face of this earth."[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Koehl#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoodrick-Clarke200218-49) His language explicitly rejected democracy as having ruined the world, citing that the victory of the [Allied powers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allies_of_World_War_II "Allies of World War II") led unfavorably to concepts he opposed such as miscegenation, [rock music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_effects_of_rock_music "Social effects of rock music"), [Alternative lifestyles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alternative_lifestyle "Alternative lifestyle"), [HIV/AIDS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HIV/AIDS "HIV/AIDS"), crime and corruption.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Koehl#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoodrick-Clarke200218-49)

In [Collection Highlights](https://sites.brown.edu/thehallhoagcollection/category/highlights/)

John Patler was born John C. Patsalos in 1938 in New York. Patler became a member of the [American Nazi Party](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party) after he was dishonorably discharged from the Marines after attending a Pro-Nazi rally.[1] Patler served as the editor of the ANP magazine “Stromtrooper” and was moving up in the ranks until he was kicked out of the group after a disagreement with ANP founder and leader [George Lincoln Rockwell](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Lincoln_Rockwell). Several months later in 1967 Patler assassinated Rockwell and was sentenced to 20 years in prison. Patler was released from prison in 1975, changed his name back to Patsalos and moved to New York. [2]

This article is about the party founded by George Lincoln Rockwell. For the 1990s National Socialist White People's Party, see [Harold Covington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harold_Covington "Harold Covington"). For the party started by Frank Collin, see [National Socialist Party of America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Socialist_Party_of_America "National Socialist Party of America").

| Party flag |
| [![Image 1: Flag of the SS with a blue dot in the center](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/82/American_Nazi_Party_flag_%28Blank_Globe%29.jpg/250px-American_Nazi_Party_flag_%28Blank_Globe%29.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:American_Nazi_Party_flag_(Blank_Globe).jpg) |
| * [Politics of the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Politics_of_the_United_States "Politics of the United States") * [Political parties](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_political_parties_in_the_United_States "List of political parties in the United States") * [Elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elections_in_the_United_States "Elections in the United States") |

The **American Nazi Party** (**ANP**) is an American [neo-Nazi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neo-Nazi "Neo-Nazi")[political party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_parties_in_the_United_States "Political parties in the United States") founded by [George Lincoln Rockwell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Lincoln_Rockwell "George Lincoln Rockwell") in 1959. In Rockwell's time, it was headquartered in [Arlington, Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arlington,_Virginia "Arlington, Virginia"). It was renamed the **National Socialist White People's Party** (**NSWPP**) in 1967. Rockwell [was murdered](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_George_Lincoln_Rockwell "Assassination of George Lincoln Rockwell") by former ANP member [John Patler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Patler "John Patler") later that year. Following Rockwell's murder, the organization appointed Rockwell's second in command, Deputy Commander [Matt Koehl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Koehl "Matt Koehl"), as the new leader.

The NSWPP, now under Koehl's command, was subject to ideological disagreements between members in the 1970s and 1980s, leading to several members being kicked out and forming their own groups. Koehl renamed the NSWPP the **New Order** in 1983, which came with a shift in the organization towards [esoteric neo-Nazism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Esoteric_neo-Nazism "Esoteric neo-Nazism"). After Koehl's death in 2014, a long-time member and officer of the New Order, [Martin Kerr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Kerr "Martin Kerr"), assumed leadership.

### Background and founding

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=American_Nazi_Party&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Background and founding")]

The American Nazi Party was founded in October 1959 by [George Lincoln Rockwell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Lincoln_Rockwell "George Lincoln Rockwell"), a commercial artist, publisher, and commander in the United States Navy. Rockwell had become radicalized into National Socialism after an initial contact with antisemitic anti-communist figures, and became a neo-Nazi after reading [Adolf Hitler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adolf_Hitler "Adolf Hitler")'s autobiography _[Mein Kampf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mein\_Kampf "Mein Kampf")_ in 1950.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoodrick-Clarke20029-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchmaltz200058-2)

After this experience, Rockwell spent several years organizing extreme right-wing political groups; he initially tried to do this in a socially acceptable fashion, but came to see this as a failure as it did not attract an extreme enough audience. He eventually decided to go public with his antisemitism, and made more extreme and explicit political efforts.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoodrick-Clarke200210%E2%80%9311-3) When Rockwell's supporters were implicated in the [Hebrew Benevolent Congregation Temple bombing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hebrew_Benevolent_Congregation_Temple_bombing "Hebrew Benevolent Congregation Temple bombing"), it caused a backlash against him, and Rockwell's wife and family cut ties with him.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoodrick-Clarke200210%E2%80%9311-3) Now miserable, Rockwell had a Nazi "religious experience" and committed to overt, explicit advocacy of Nazism.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoodrick-Clarke200211-4) In October 1959, Rockwell founded the American Nazi Party.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchmaltz200058-2)

[![Image 2: refer to caption](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b6/Martin_Luther_King_Jr_after_he_was_punched_by_neo-Nazi_Roy_James.png/250px-Martin_Luther_King_Jr_after_he_was_punched_by_neo-Nazi_Roy_James.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Martin_Luther_King_Jr_after_he_was_punched_by_neo-Nazi_Roy_James.png)

[Martin Luther King Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Luther_King_Jr. "Martin Luther King Jr.") (left) gesturing at Roy James (right) after James punched him in the face; in the center, breaking them up, is [Ralph Abernathy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ralph_Abernathy "Ralph Abernathy")

Its headquarters were established at 928 North Randolph Street in Arlington, which also became Rockwell's home, and a nearby farmhouse served as a barracks for its members.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoodrick-Clarke200211-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party#cite_note-FOOTNOTESimonelli199940-5) Under Rockwell, the party explicitly embraced Nazi uniforms and [iconography](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nazi_Party#Party_symbols "Nazi Party"), and embarked on high profile media stunts designed to gain the maximum amount of press coverage.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGreenStabler2015390-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoodrick-Clarke200212-7) The group itself was quite fringe and had few members in comparison with the very large amount of publicity it garnered.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoodrick-Clarke200212-7) Members regularly protested and caused disruptions.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoodrick-Clarke200213-8)

The [Virginia House of Delegates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virginia_House_of_Delegates "Virginia House of Delegates") revoked the ANP's corporation charter in June 1962 and banned the use of the name "Nazi" or "National Socialist" in charter names. A new charter was submitted under the name of ANP, Inc., which was rejected on a technicality. It was recreated under the name the George Lincoln Rockwell Party with only a single change on the board of directors.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchmaltz2000145-9)

In September 1962, ANP member Roy James punched [Martin Luther King Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Luther_King_Jr. "Martin Luther King Jr.") twice while King was speaking at a convention. King did not defend himself and instead spoke to him.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party#cite_note-:2-10)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoodrick-Clarke200213-8)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party#cite_note-11) James expressed regret and apologized shortly after the attack, but later went back on it.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party#cite_note-:2-10)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party#cite_note-12) James was sentenced to 30 days in jail and fined $25 (equal to $259.87 today) after pleading guilty to charge of assault and battery and disorderly conduct. King had not wanted to press charges, but Birmingham Judge Charles H. Brown insisted on trying James, calling the incident an "uncalled for, unprovoked assault."[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party#cite_note-13) In September 1962, Rockwell awarded James a medal for the deed.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoodrick-Clarke200213-8)

In November 1963, when King was set to speak in [Danville, Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danville,_Virginia "Danville, Virginia"), to set up a dialogue with whites, Rockwell sent ANP member [Karl Allen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Allen "Karl Allen") and another member to instigate against him.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchmaltz2000193-14)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party#cite_note-FOOTNOTESimonelli199976-15) He initially planned to have Allen stay there for some time to harass King, but this plan was derailed by the [Kennedy assassination](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_assassination "Kennedy assassination").[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchmaltz2000193%E2%80%93194-16)

Rockwell's money habits and usage of the ANP's funding resulted in regular problems for the party and rough conditions for its members.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchmaltz2000177%E2%80%93178-17) Many became dissatisfied with his leadership.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchmaltz2000195%E2%80%93196-18) The second highest ranking member, Karl Allen, left the ANP in December, claiming it was for personal reasons.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchmaltz2000195-19) This surprised Rockwell, and he was disturbed to lose the best educated member of the group and second in command. Many party members left and followed Allen, and drew up a list of grievances against Rockwell and his leadership tactics, particularly an inability to "refrain from inserting his personality and judgment into every minute part of the Party's operation". They enumerated a list of grievances to be addressed and changes in the party's operations if they were to rejoin.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchmaltz2000195%E2%80%93196-18) Rockwell refused to address the demands. He was most worried about a demand that he would no longer have sole discretion over the board of directors, which he worried would be used to take control of the party. From then on declared them to be "the mutiny" and kept them out of the ANP.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchmaltz2000196-20)

After several years of living in impoverished conditions, Rockwell began to experience some financial success with paid speaking engagements at universities where he was invited to express his controversial views as exercises in free speech. This prompted him to end the rancorous "Phase One" party tactics and begin "Phase Two", a plan to recast the group as a legitimate political party by toning down the verbal and written attacks against non-whites, replacing the party rallying cry of "[Sieg Heil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sieg_Heil "Sieg Heil")!" with "White Power!", limiting public display of the swastika, and entering candidates in local elections.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGreenStabler2015390-6)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKaplan20001%E2%80%933-21)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoodrick-Clarke200214-22)

During the 1960s, the FBI's COINTELPRO "White Hate" program placed the ANP under surveillance and undertook operations aimed at discrediting and disrupting its activities as part of a broader targeting of white supremacist and extremist groups.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party#cite_note-23)

The years 1965 and 1967 were possibly the height of Rockwell's profile.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKaplan20001%E2%80%933-21) He was interviewed by _[Playboy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Playboy "Playboy")_ magazine, an event that stirred controversy within the ranks.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKaplan20001%E2%80%933-21) At the time Rockwell had about 500 followers.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGreenStabler2015390-6)

### Name change and assassination of Rockwell

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=American_Nazi_Party&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Name change and assassination of Rockwell")]

On January 1, 1967, the group underwent several changes. Rockwell changed the name of the American Nazi Party to the National Socialist White People's Party (NSWPP), changed the logo to a stylized [eagle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eagle "Eagle"), and replaced their slogan of [Sieg Heil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sieg_Heil "Sieg Heil") with White Power, all in an effort to Americanize the organization and increase its appeal.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchmaltz2000304-24) This alienated some hard-line members. The new name was a "conscious imitation" of the [National Association for the Advancement of Colored People](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Association_for_the_Advancement_of_Colored_People "National Association for the Advancement of Colored People"). Rockwell wanted a more "ecumenical" approach and felt that the swastika banner was impeding organizational growth. Rockwell was killed on August 25, 1967, before he could implement party reforms.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGreenStabler2015390-6)

On August 25, 1967, as Rockwell left a laundromat, a former follower named [John Patler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Patler "John Patler")[shot Rockwell from the roof of the building](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_George_Lincoln_Rockwell "Assassination of George Lincoln Rockwell"). One bullet missed, the other hit his chest and ruptured his heart. He was pronounced dead at the scene.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchmaltz2013-25)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party#cite_note-26)

### Koehl's succession and ideological divisions

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=American_Nazi_Party&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Koehl's succession and ideological divisions")]

Rockwell's second in command, Deputy Commander [Matt Koehl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Koehl "Matt Koehl"), a staunch [Hitlerist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hitler "Hitler"), assumed the leadership role after a council agreed that he should retain command. In 1968, Koehl moved the party to a new headquarters on 2507 North Franklin Road, clearly visible from [Arlington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arlington,_Virginia "Arlington, Virginia")'s main thoroughfare, Wilson Boulevard.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchmaltz2013344-27) In 1969, NSWPP [William Luther Pierce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Luther_Pierce "William Luther Pierce") and [Joseph Tommasi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Tommasi "Joseph Tommasi") founded the [National Socialist Liberation Front](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Socialist_Liberation_Front "National Socialist Liberation Front") (NSLF) as a youth wing of the American Nazi Party, aiming for it to appeal to White college students.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKaplan200098,_221,_302-28) In 1970, [David Duke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Duke "David Duke") joined the NSLF youth wing (through mail order).[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKaplan200098-29)

Koehl's leadership style resulted in many members leaving the group or being kicked out.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKaplan2000155-30) The party began to experience ideological divisions among its followers as it entered the 1970s.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchmaltz2013346-31) Thereafter, the members engaged in internecine disputes, and they were either expelled by Koehl or they resigned. After the murder of Rockwell, the party dissipated and ad hoc organizations usurped the American Nazi Party logo. Those included James Burford in Chicago and John Bishop in Iowa.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKaplan20001%E2%80%933-21) Some members of the NSWPP chose to support William Luther Pierce, who was kicked out by Koehl,[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party#cite_note-FOOTNOTESunshine202435-32) and formed the [National Alliance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Alliance_(United_States) "National Alliance (United States)") in 1974.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchmaltz2013346-31) Others went with Joseph Tommasi, who was abruptly kicked out of the group for unclear reasons by Koehl in 1973.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKaplan2000174,_247,_302-33)[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party#cite_note-FOOTNOTESunshine202426,_36-34) Tommasi founded the National Socialist Liberation Front in 1974, using the same name as the NSWPP's youth wing, but in effect an entirely new group.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKaplan2000155-30)[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party#cite_note-FOOTNOTESunshine202437-35) The new NSLF was a highly militant splinter of the NSWPP that attracted its most radical members; members were linked to several violent attacks.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKaplan2000222-36)

In 1975, members of the California NSWPP were the subject of the academy award nominee documentary film _[The California Reich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_California\_Reich "The California Reich")_.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party#cite_note-37)

In 1982 the [Internal Revenue Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internal_Revenue_Service "Internal Revenue Service") took action to foreclose on the group's headquarters in Arlington, Virginia.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKaplan2000156-38) The site of the party headquarters, 928 North Randolph Street in [Ballston, Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ballston,_Virginia "Ballston, Virginia"), is now a hotel and office building. After Rockwell's death, his successor [Matt Koehl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Koehl "Matt Koehl") relocated the headquarters to 2507 North Franklin Road in [Clarendon, Arlington, Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clarendon,_Arlington,_Virginia "Clarendon, Arlington, Virginia").[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party#cite_note-39) The small building, often misidentified today as Rockwell's former headquarters became The Java Shack.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party#cite_note-40)[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party#cite_note-41)

Koehl's NSWPP changed its name to New Order on January 1, 1983, on the grounds that the people in the area "are not people looking to join revolutionary organizations", saying that it was moving to an area in the Midwest which it would not reveal for security reasons.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party#cite_note-42) This was announced by [Martin Kerr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Kerr "Martin Kerr"), the leader at the Franklin Road headquarters.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party#cite_note-northernvirginiamag-43) Due to recruitment issues along with financial and legal trouble, Koehl was forced to relocate the group's headquarters from the DC area, eventually finding his way to scattered locations in [Wisconsin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wisconsin "Wisconsin") and [Michigan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan "Michigan").[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party#cite_note-:0-44) The name change reflected the group's [neo-Nazi mysticism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neo-Nazi_mysticism "Neo-Nazi mysticism") and it was still known by that name in 2010.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party#cite_note-northernvirginiamag-43)

The organization briefly attracted the media's attention in October 1983, when it held a private meeting at [Yorktown High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yorktown_High_School_(Virginia) "Yorktown High School (Virginia)") in Arlington, Virginia.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party#cite_note-45) New Order's Chief of Staff, Martin Kerr, claims that the group is no longer a [white supremacist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_supremacist "White supremacist") group and focuses on advocating "in favor of [white] people, not against other races or ethnicities...we consider the white people of the world to be a gigantic family of racial brothers and sisters, united by ties of common ancestry and common heritage. Being for our own family does not mean that we hate other families." The SPLC still classifies them as neo-Nazis and as a "hate group".[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party#cite_note-46)[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party#cite_note-47)[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party#cite_note-48) After Koehl's death in 2014, Kerr assumed leadership and maintains the New Order website and organization.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party#cite_note-:0-44)

The American Nazi Party's flag was a standard [Nazi flag](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nazi_flag "Nazi flag") with a small blue dot in the center,[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party#cite_note-FOOTNOTEThayer196821-49)[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKaplan2000562-50) supposed to represent a globe, which it was in some iterations.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party#cite_note-:1-51) An ANP storm trooper meeting with journalist George Thayer explained that this blue dot was supposed to be representative of the [United Nations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations "United Nations") being consumed by Nazism.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party#cite_note-FOOTNOTEThayer196821-49) In a 1967 issue of the ANP's _[The Stormtrooper Magazine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Stormtrooper\_Magazine "The Stormtrooper Magazine")_, the party stated the blue dot was added to symbolize internationalism and non-German white races, in which they differed from the original Nazis, to "represent the world and all the White People who live in the world".[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party#cite_note-:1-51) After Rockwell was assassinated, the blue dot was removed from the party's flag and they began using a standard Nazi flag; an internal memo reproduced by [James K. Warner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_K._Warner "James K. Warner") in his 1968 "open letter" declared that the "pure Aryan Swastika of our ancestors is to be used unblemished."[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKaplan2000562-50)

The ANP published several periodicals, run on a subscription, which it used to connect with the party's various sympathizers. The sympathizers sometimes became members or followers of the group.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchmaltz200073-52) Its first periodical, the _National Socialist Bulletin_, was founded in May 1960; it was a small periodical, 15 pages long for each issue. It published eight issues, before it was succeeded by _[The Stormtrooper Magazine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Stormtrooper\_Magazine "The Stormtrooper Magazine")_.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchmaltz200073-52) They also ran _The Rockwell Report_, starting in 1961; the _Report_, unlike the Bulletin, was a full-size magazine.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchmaltz2000128-53)

Rockwell and some party members established a "Stormtrooper Barracks" in an old mansion owned by the widow of Willis Kern[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchmaltz2013-25) in the Dominion Hills section of Arlington at what is now the [Upton Hill Regional Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Upton_Hill_Regional_Park "Upton Hill Regional Park"). After Rockwell's murder, the headquarters was moved again to one side of a duplex brick and concrete storefront at 2507 North Franklin Road which featured a [swastika](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swastika "Swastika") prominently mounted above the front door. This site was visible from busy Wilson Boulevard. Today, the Franklin Road address is often misidentified as Rockwell's headquarters when in fact it was the successor organization's last physical address in Arlington (now a coffeehouse).[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party#cite_note-Fenston-54)[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party#cite_note-55)[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party#cite_note-56)

The ANP also had three other chapters in cities outside of the main organization in Arlington: in Los Angeles, Chicago, and Dallas.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchmaltz2000230-57)[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party#cite_note-FOOTNOTESimonelli199949-58)

In 1962, Rockwell established the Western Division,[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchmaltz2000135-59) also called the Western Division—ANP,[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchmaltz2000139-60) as the California or West Coast branch of the ANP.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKaplan2000112,_156-61) Relative to even the rest of the ANP, it was known as especially fractious, with it being plagued by numerous schisms and leadership disputes.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKaplan2000111%E2%80%93112-62) At least half of all members of this division had either felony arrests or had been institutionalized for mental health reasons.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party#cite_note-FOOTNOTESimonelli199935-63)

Rockwell made serious efforts to organize the division for two years.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party#cite_note-FOOTNOTESimonelli199935-63) It was initially led by Leonard Holstein. However, in 1963 Holstein was jailed after a riot involving several party members and a group of Jews. Rockwell then replaced Holstein with [Ralph Perry Forbes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ralph_Perry_Forbes "Ralph Perry Forbes") in May 1963.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchmaltz2000174-64) The Western Division relocated to [Glendale, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glendale,_California "Glendale, California") in late 1964 and afterwards Forbes and other ANP members became involved in a dispute with the city. The Glendale authorities attempted to evict them and the city refused to turn on the electricity unless Forbes signed an [affidavit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Affidavit "Affidavit") promising to not use the house for Nazi activities, which Forbes refused. Forbes said that his lease allowed him to use the property for political purposes, which the homeowner had thought was the [Republican](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republican_Party_(United_States) "Republican Party (United States)") or [Democratic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Party_(United_States) "Democratic Party (United States)") political parties, not the Nazi Party. The city then filed a complaint against Forbes for "operating a meeting hall in a single-family dwelling without a permit"; this dispute eventually escalated to also involve [Los Angeles County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles_County "Los Angeles County").[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchmaltz2000229-65) His eviction was stayed later that year and he was allowed to live in his home until the expiration of the lease; his landlord was instead ordered to pay for his eviction proceedings.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchmaltz2000251-66) In 1966, the Western Division moved to [El Monte, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Monte,_California "El Monte, California") after the rent on their headquarters increased four times over.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchmaltz2000279-67)[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party#cite_note-FOOTNOTECady202063-68)[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchmaltz2000293-69)

In late 1968,[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKaplan2000156-38) the conflict between the secular stance of the ANP and Forbes's beliefs (Forbes was a [Christian Identity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christian_Identity "Christian Identity") adherent) came to the forefront, with his legitimacy as a leader now in question without Rockwell. Members Allen Vincent and [James K. Warner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_K._Warner "James K. Warner") led a schism within the Western Division, and Rockwell's successor [Matt Koehl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Koehl "Matt Koehl") had to travel to California to mediate it. Koehl decided Forbes should be the legitimate leader; in response, members rebelled.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKaplan2000111%E2%80%93112-62) This resulted in numerous schisms from the Western Division.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKaplan2000111%E2%80%93112-62) Later that year, Forbes was ousted by the Western Division and later left the ANP.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKaplan2000112-70) Forbes was eventually succeeded by [Joseph Tommasi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Tommasi "Joseph Tommasi"), who was also ousted from the group and founded his own schism party, the NSLF.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party#cite_note-FOOTNOTECady202065-71) After his murder, the Western Division exited El Monte. They planned to move out of El Monte and to Pasadena, but there is no evidence they did so.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party#cite_note-72)[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party#cite_note-FOOTNOTECady202065%E2%80%9366-73)

The Chicago unit of the ANP was established in 1962.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party#cite_note-FOOTNOTESimonelli199978-74) It was founded out of what had started as an ANP front organization, established in 1960, the Fighting American Nationalists (FAN). FAN also had branches in other states.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party#cite_note-FOOTNOTESimonelli1999100-75)

By 1962, the Chicago FAN unit, which was the largest, turned into simply another branch of the ANP.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchmaltz2000133-76) They owned a small bookstore called the Vineland Bookstore and were headquartered in a two-story brick building.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchmaltz2000133-76) Its first leader was Eugene "Mal" Lambert and Matt Koehl, before Koehl was transferred to the main Arlington faction in February 1963.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchmaltz2000133-76)[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party#cite_note-FOOTNOTESimonelli199978-74) That year, they lost their headquarters on account of building code violations.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchmaltz2000183,_197-77) They opened another in December 1964.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchmaltz2000230-57) This unit had the only woman to have a position of power in the group, Erika Himmler.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party#cite_note-FOOTNOTESimonelli1999164-78) Chris Vidnjevich was in charge by 1965.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchmaltz2000244-79)

The Chicago unit was a target of a two-part plot by COINTELPRO in 1965, attempting to disrupt their leadership and destroy them financially. They recruited a member of the Anti-Defamation League to enact this plan, and the FBI sent fake letters to local Jewish organizations in an attempt to get the city to take action against them.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchmaltz2000243%E2%80%93244-80) During the ANP's high profile 1966 White power protests in Chicago, possibly the height of the ANP's success, Vidnjevich and the Chicago ANP were heavily involved.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchmaltz2000287-81) After Rockwell died, the unit was shut down during Koehl's leadership.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchmaltz2000335-82)

The Dallas unit of the ANP was established in November 1964. It was primarily led by Robert Surrey (aka Max Amann), a former member of the John Birch Society, and his wife, Mary Surrey. Robert Surrey was a major patron of the party.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchmaltz2000225,_256-83)[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party#cite_note-FOOTNOTESimonelli199940%E2%80%9341-84) This one was structured differently than the others, split into a "social group", led by the Surreys and a stormtrooper group led by Jerald Walraven. This was done in order to protect the reputations of those wealthy supporters in the social group who paid for the stormtroopers. The social group met with the Surreys and the Stormtrooper outfit instead met at a different Dallas headquarters.[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchmaltz2000225-85) The Dallas unit participated in Rockwell's agitation campaigns,[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchmaltz2000253-86) and anti-racial integration demonstrations.[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchmaltz2000256-87) After Rockwell's death, Robert Surrey left the party and wrote a memorandum denouncing Koehl.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party#cite_note-FOOTNOTESimonelli199949-58)

Namesake organizations
----------------------

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=American_Nazi_Party&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Namesake organizations")]

Since the late 1960s, there have been a number of small unrelated groups that have used the name "American Nazi Party".

*   Perhaps the first was led by James Warner and Allen Vincent and it consisted of members of the California branch of the NSWPP.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKaplan20001%E2%80%933,_558%E2%80%93562-88) This group announced its existence on January 1, 1968. In 1982 James Burford formed another "American Nazi Party" from disaffected branches of the [National Socialist Party of America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Socialist_Party_of_America "National Socialist Party of America").[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKaplan20003,_33-89) This Chicago-based group remained in existence until at least 1994.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party#cite_note-90)[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party#cite_note-91)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKaplan20001%E2%80%933-21)
*   A small American Nazi Party, operating out of [Davenport, Iowa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Davenport,_Iowa "Davenport, Iowa"), under the leadership of John Robert Bishop, maintained a presence until its eventual decline in 1985.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party#cite_note-92)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKaplan20001%E2%80%933-21)[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMarks199658-93)
*   A former member of the original American Nazi Party, [Rocky Suhayda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rocky_Suhayda "Rocky Suhayda"), founded his own organization using the American Nazi Party name and has been active since at least 2008.[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party#cite_note-94)
*   [Harold Covington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harold_Covington "Harold Covington") also ran a group that took the name National Socialist White People's Party.[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Nazi_Party#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKaplan2000228-95)

# Introduction 

This study analyzes the leadership style, impact, and enduring legacies of three crucial leaders in the 

white supremacist and neo -Nazi movements: Louis Beam, William Luther Pierce, and James Mason. 

It examines the interplay of leadership traits, significant events in the life narratives of the leader, and 

the legacies of these three key pioneers towards two aims. First, our analysis draws on the CIP 

Leadership Framework and charismatic leadership studie s to assess the respective leadership roles of 

Beam, Pierce, and Mason. Second, it considers how the leadership traits and ideological impact of 

these leaders shaped contemporary far -right movements in the United States (U.S.), as well as how 

the legacies of these figures can be observed in the modern far -right landscape. Overall, we argue that 

the three leaders profiled herein cover the full leadership spectrum of the CIP framework and that each 

was both a product and exploiter of their life narratives in ways that fundamentally shaped their 

leadership style, impact, and legacy on the American far -right landscape. 

This study begins by establishing the foundation for the conceptual framework through which the 

authors analyze the leadership and impact of Be am, Pierce, and Mason. It draws on the Ligon et al .

CIP (Charismatic, Ideological, and Pragmatic) leadership model with its dual focus on leadership 

typologies and six life events that tend to characterize the life narratives of outstanding leaders. Our 

fr amework is further supplemented by a more nuanced conceptual grounding in charismatic leadership 

theory. It then features the three central case studies. These case studies seek to examine the 

respective backgrounds, leadership styles, influence, and last ing appeal of these American ideologues. 

It traces their life experiences, reviewing the totality of their contributions to their respective far -right 

milieus. In doing so, it examines their roles within specific right -wing movements as well as their roles 

as nodes that connected disparate elements of the modern far -right. This study concludes by drawing 

out key overarching findings that emerge from the preceding analysis. Specifically, it focuses on the 

enduring legacies of Beam, Pierce, and Mason by refle cting on how they have collectively impacted 

the evolution of violent far -right movements, and considers how the differences in the leadership types 

and life narratives have shaped that legacy. Finally, it offers policy insights and avenues for future 

rese arch with respect to the modern far -right landscape and the role of charismatic leadership in 

prominent white supremacist movements active today. Lewis & Ingram • June 2023 

Founding Fathers of the Modern American Neo -Nazi Movement 7

# Leadership Types, Life Narratives, and Charisma 

A major focus of leadership studies is to distinguish between different types of leadership to understand 

how and why leaders emerge, particularly in relation to organizational and broader contextual factors. 

A variety of different factors may be used to d istinguish between different ideal types of leadership, but 

the most important factor is arguably what characterizes the leader -follower relationship. After all, it is 

a mix of psychosocial, organizational, and strategic factors that fuse with how the lead er presents 

themselves (the leader’s image) and their message (the leader’s narratives) that are crucial to forging 

leader -follower bonds. This study adopts a larger, top -down, leader -centric approach to understanding 

the leadership styles of three promine nt figures in the American far -right milieu. In doing so, it promises 

to draw out important insights into those crucial bottom -up, contextual, and follower -centric factors that 

are vital for understanding the influence of such leaders. 

This study is the second in a series of Program on Extremism papers that analyze the leadership of 

American violent extremists. The first study, titled The Founding Fathers of American Jihad , analyzed 

the leadership and influence of Americans Anwar al -Awlaki, Samir Khan, a nd Ahmad Abousamra. The 

study argued that “distinctions in leadership styles are reflective of the different personal attributes, 

backgrounds, and organizational contexts within which the individuals operated. Moreover, these 

differences in leadership char acteristics shaped their respective impacts and legacies in ways that have 

important implications for the fields of research and practice.” 1 For conceptual and analytical 

consistency, this study applies the same conceptual framework by drawing on the Ligo n et al . CIP 

(Charismatic, Ideological, and Pragmatic) framework and charismatic leadership studies. 2

Case Study Application 

The CIP model offers a comprehensive and versatile framework covering charismatic, ideological, and 

pragmatic leadership ideal types . The authors distinguish between the three typologies by arguing that 

while the pragmatic leader tends to focus on short -te rm problems and immediate solutions, the other 

leadership types are visionaries with the charismatic leader offering “a passionate vision of a future 

radically different from present conditions…. if [followers] accept the leader’s movement, ” and the 

ideolo gical leader tending to project “personal values and beliefs” to motivate followers and make

> Samir Khan, and Ahmad Abousamra (Washington, D.C.: Program on Extremism, June 2021): 2,
> https://extremism.gwu.edu/sites/g/files/zaxdzs2191/f/The%20Founding%20Fathers%20of%20American%20Jihad.pdf .
> 2Gina Scott Ligon, Samuel T. Hunter, and Michael D. Mumford, “Developmen t of outstanding leadership: A life narrative

> Relationship: Alternative Explanations and Predictions,” Leadership Quarterly 2, no. 2 (1991): 81 –104 ; Shmuel Eisenstadt,
> “Charisma and Institution Building: Max Weber and Modern Sociology,” In Power Trust and Meaning (Chicago: The
> University of Chicago Press, 1995): 167 –201 ; Alan Bryman, Charisma and Leadership in Organizations (London : Sage,
